    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Reason ↗ Open Full Page

    En Banc Fifth Circuit Declares House COVID Proxy Voting Rule Unconstitutional

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1698 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that today, in Texas v.
    • The opinion, by Judge Wilson, joined by Chief Judge Elrod and Judges Jones, Smith, Willett, Ho, Duncan, Engelhardt, and Oldham begins:.
    • Industry observers note that during the COVID-19 pandemic, the House of Representatives adopted a rule allowing Members to record their presence by proxy for purposes of establishing a quorum.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that today, in Texas v. Blanche, the en banc U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit concluded that the proxy voting rule adopted by the House of Representatives during the COVID-19 pandemic violated the Quorum Clause.

    The opinion, by Judge Wilson, joined by Chief Judge Elrod and Judges Jones, Smith, Willett, Ho, Duncan, Engelhardt, and Oldham begins:.

    Industry observers note that during the COVID-19 pandemic, the House of Representatives adopted a rule allowing Members to record their presence by proxy for purposes of establishing a quorum. The House used this rule when passing the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2023 (the Act), having mustered a quorum by counting hundreds of otherwise absent Members as present by proxy. The Senate then passed the bill, and the President signed it into law.

    In a recent development, the State of Texas argues that the House's proxy-presence rule is inconsistent with the Constitution's Quorum Clause, which would mean that the House did not validly pass the Act. See U.S. Const. art. I, § 5, cl. 1. Based on that proposition, Texas seeks injunctive relief against just one portion of the Act: The Pregnant Workers Fairness Act (PWFA). The federal Government responds that the enrolled-bill rule, which instructs that a bill's passage through the legislature is conclusive proof of its authenticity, precludes judicial review of whether the Act's passage complied with the Quorum Clause. Alternatively, the Government argues that the Quorum Clause permits proxy presence.

    The district court held that the enrolled-bill rule did not apply and that the House's passage of the Act—through use of the proxy-presence rule —violated the Quorum Clause. Accordingly, the district court enjoined the Government from enforcing the PWFA against Texas.

    We conclude that the enrolled-bill rule does not bar our review because Texas's constitutional challenge does not implicate a dispute of fact regarding the Act's passage. We further conclude that the Act's passage was unconstitutional because the Quorum Clause does not allow proxies to be included when establishing a quorum. The Clause's text, context, original understanding, and unbroken historical application all indicate that Members of Congress must be present for quorum purposes—as the Supreme Court expressly held over 125 years ago, and as Congress has done ever since the Founding. "Proxy presence" does not count. While the chambers of the legislature have much discretion regarding their rules of procedure, the Quorum Clause's constraints on congressional power cannot be circumvented by congressional fiat. We therefore affirm the judgment of the district court.

    The enrolled-bill doctrine articulated in Marshall Field does not preclude judicial review of Texas's Quorum Clause challenge. There are no disputed facts regarding the House's passage of the Act such that we would need to sift any extrinsic evidence. On the contrary, the parties agree that the House purportedly established a quorum only because it counted hundreds of proxies as "present." Texas's challenge therefore depends solely on the Quorum Clause's proper meaning.

    Through that lens, the House's passage of the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2023 contravened the Quorum Clause. The Clause's text, context, original understanding, and historical application all indicate that proxies may not be counted to establish a quorum. As the Supreme Court has held, and as Congress had previously done for over 230 years, Members must be present to satisfy the Quorum Clause. Presence-by-proxy does not suffice. An absent Member's assignment of his or her proxy cannot render that Member present for purposes of the Quorum Clause. Texas has carried its burden to show that it is entitled to a permanent injunction against the PWFA.

    Industry observers note that judge Graves wrote the dissent, joined by Judges Stewart, Richman, Southwick, Higginson, Douglas, and Ramirez. It begins:.

    In this suit, the State of Texas sought a preliminary injunction preventing enforcement of one portion of the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2023, the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act (PWFA), attempting to veto Congress's protections for pregnant workers and new parents while retaining millions in federal funding.

    It has been revealed that on May 15, 2020, in response to the COVID-19 pandemic, the House of Representatives adopted House Resolution 965, which authorized remote committee proceedings and remote voting in the House. Resolution 965 provides that:.

    1. [A]t any time after the Speaker . . . is notified . . . that a public health emergency due to a novel coronavirus is in effect, the Speaker . . . may designate a period . . . during which a Member who is designated by another Member as proxy in accordance with section 2 may cast the vote of such other Member or record the presence of such other Member in the House.

    H.R. Res. 965 § 1(a), 116th Cong. (2020).

    Section 2 described the process for remote participation through designating proxies: the designating Member had to submit a signed letter to the Clerk that specified the designated Member. Id. § 2. Section 3 outlined the process for voting during covered periods, which, absent an extension, ran for forty-five days after the Speaker, or their designee, designated such a period. Id. §§ 1(b), 3. Section 4 authorized remote Committee proceedings. Id. § 4. Section 5 mandated that the chair of the Committee on House Administration certify that it would be feasible to use technology to conduct remote voting in the House, required that the chair of the Committee on Rules submit regulations providing for the implementation of remote voting, and provided for remote voting once those regulations were in place. Id. § 5. Section 6 required that Sections 1, 2, and 3 be carried out in accordance with existing House rules to the extent practicable. Id. § 6. During the 117th Congress, the House reaffirmed this practice in House Resolution 8 and continued to apply it. H.R. Res. 8 § 3(s), 117th Cong. (2021).

    According to recent reports, at matter here: the House used these procedures as it voted on and passed the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2023. See 168 Cong. Rec. H10,529 (daily ed. Dec. 23, 2022). Under House rules, a quorum of the 435-Member House is a simple majority: 218. See, e.g., Rules of the House of Representatives, R. XX, cl. 6(b), H.R. Doc. No. 116-177, at 873–74 (2021). The vote on the final passage of the Act was 225 yeas, 201 nays, 1 "present," and 4 non-votes. 168 Cong. Rec. H10,528 (daily ed. Dec. 23, 2022). Out of the 431 votes, 205 votes were cast by Members in person and 226 were cast remotely by proxy. See id. at H10,529.

    It has been revealed that even though less than a majority was physically present at the time of the vote, no Member objected that a quorum was lacking. Id. Representative Chip Roy of Texas, however, noted that a physical quorum was not present and reserved the right to object. Id. In response to a series of parliamentary inquiries from Representative Roy as to how a quorum was present, the Speaker Pro Tempore, Representative G.K. Butterfield, responded that a quorum was present because "Members casting their vote or recording their presence by proxy [we]re counted for the purpose of establishing a quorum" pursuant to House Resolution 8. Id.

    After the Act passed the House, presiding officers of both chambers of Congress printed and signed the bill. See 1 U.S.C. § 106. At that point, it was an "enrolled bill." Id. The enrolled bill was then sent to the President, who signed the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2023 into law. See Pub. L. No. 117-328, 136 Stat. 4459 (2022).

    The $1.7 trillion-dollar government funding bill was passed in accordance with House Rules, including House Resolution 8, which allowed members to record their presence remotely by proxy during the coronavirus pandemic. 431 votes were cast with respect to the bill. At the time, no Member objected that a quorum was lacking. Nonetheless, the State of Texas, having accepted the vast majority of the funds that Congress appropriated to it, now contends that the portion of the bill providing protections for pregnant women and workers violates the Quorum Clause.

    Texas contends that the Act is invalid because the Quorum Clause required that a majority of Members be physically present on the House floor at the time of the vote. In so doing, Texas asks the courts to graft an additional requirement to the Quorum Clause of the Constitution.

    Recent findings suggest that I agree with the majority that the enrolled-bill rule does not bar our review of this particular constitutional challenge. However, I cannot agree with their addition of a new requirement to the Quorum Clause. Even though the majority declares that its reasoning is limited to the question of "whether the Quorum Clause allows proxy presence to be included in the quorum count," ante at 17–18, their conclusion is far more expansive. The conclusion that "[t]he Quorum Clause is concerned with physical presence" shoehorns a much larger requirement into the Constitution. Ante at 28. Because the plain text of Article I, Section 5, Clause 1, historical practice, and evidence of the framers' intent all weigh against the addition of the majority's new "physical presence" requirement, I respectfully dissent.

    Judge Haynes did not join the dissent, but a footnote to the opinion reads:.

    Judge Haynes states that she does not think it is appropriate to throw out the Federal House of Representatives in this arena, so she dissents. She also appreciates Judge Graves's dissent.

    Although the majority purports to offer a narrow holding, and only blocks enforcement of the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act in Texas, the opinions rationale would provide a basis for invalidating everything else in the omnibus bill, which included everything from the ban on using TikTok on government devices to the Electoral Count Reform and Presidential Transition Improvement Act.

    In a recent development, I doubt this decision will stand. I am not sure the Quorum Clause is justiciable, and I cannot see the Supreme Court upending all of the affected legislation on this basis.

    Recent findings suggest that the petition for certiorari in this case writes itself. Another wild card is that the latest Attorney General of Texas may not press its case.

    More from Derek Muller on Election Law Blog.

They provided excellent grip for wet items. The touch-screen feature worked well, and the snug, low-profile fit allowed us to pick up a key that was lying flat on a countertop.     Leather work gloves are a necessity when working near hot surfaces and sparks in addition to protecting the hands from abrasion, cuts, and punctures. These gloves, which have earned American National Standards Institute (ANSI) compliance for welding, provide Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA)-approved protection for a wide range of tasks. They’re waterproof and have a nose wipe on the thumb, making them a good choice for working in rough weather.

    Cold Snap gloves feature some of Carhartt’s proprietary materials, including a FastDry lining for wicking moisture and Storm Defender waterproofing treatment.     Industry observers note that we selected and tested a diverse assortment of waterproof gloves designed for a variety of uses in different seasons. For all of them, our key testing consideration was whether the gloves were truly waterproof. To find out, we used three testing methods and allowed the gloves to thoroughly dry between tests. All comments about sizing are subjective, based on sizing guides provided by the manufacturers and perceived comfort by the tester. On those gloves not listed as unisex, women tested women’s gloves, and men tested men’s gloves.

    In a recent development, first, we simulated storm conditions with a rain-wand attachment on a garden hose. The testers wore each pair of gloves beneath a steady 2-minute shower, flexing their hands and turning them over to expose all parts of the gloves to the stream. In the second test, we immersed our gloved hands into a bucket of water, again flexing and rotating to ensure that they were completely wet. Finally, we tested them for wet-gripping ability while handling smooth wet stones. To merit inclusion in this guide, each pair of gloves passed all three tests with minimal water intrusion to the inside of the glove.

    Before shopping for the best waterproof gloves, consider the type of work planned for the gloves as well as the kind of materials and construction desired. In this section, we review some key considerations to keep in mind while shopping for the best waterproof gloves, including materials, use, fit, and more.

    Sources indicate that choosing the best waterproof gloves depends on how they’ll be used. Work gloves are completely different from those intended for outdoor sports or casual wear.

    On garments labeled “waterproof,” the outer shell is usually where the magic happens. Materials like tightly woven nylon, polyester, softshell technical materials, treated leather, and others work well to shed water before it can seep through to the lining. Keep in mind that it’s very rare for leather gloves to actually be waterproof; more likely, they are simply water-resistant.

    Recent findings suggest that aside from shell material, other elements in waterproof gloves’ exteriors make them useful in wet or messy situations. Some of the best waterproof gloves, for example, have textured grips that make it easier for the wearer to grab on to wet, slippery surfaces, making them ideal for skiing, cycling, and other active pursuits. Those looking for waterproof gloves for work may want to invest in gloves with reinforced palms and thumbs, which should last longer and stand up to more wear.

    The best waterproof gloves contain an optional outer shell with conductors that transfer the electrical charge from a finger to a touch screen, allowing owners to manipulate their phones without removing their gloves.

    According to recent reports, some of the best waterproof gloves contain insulation that captures body heat, which forms air pockets that warm with the heat from the hand. Most insulation is a man-made poly-fill material such as Thinsulate or 3M.

    It has been revealed that to ensure gloves keep warm air inside and cold air from seeping in, some waterproof gloves have long elastic cuffs that hug tight to the wrist and arm, closing off any pathway for air to enter. For even warmer gloves, look for removable liners that can slip inside a waterproof glove to add another layer of insulation.

    According to recent reports, when selecting the best waterproof gloves, fit and comfort are essential. However, a “good fit” is relative to the activity. A pair of running gloves fits quite differently than a pair of winter work gloves or ski gloves.

    Waterproof running or hiking gloves often feel like a stretchy, flexible second skin. Because they’re lightweight and wick away moisture, consumers sometimes forget they’re even wearing them.

    Waterproof work gloves are bulkier and a bit stiff because they’re generally made from thick nylon or leather that resists ripping, tearing, and friction. Moreover, extra padding or reinforcement on the thumbs or palms can add to their bulk. Though work gloves fit loosely, they shouldn’t be so loose that it’s difficult to pick up small items while wearing them.

    Recent findings suggest that ski gloves are flexible but don’t wear particularly well because they’re typically made from materials like nylon. Properly fitting ski gloves fit snugly around the wrist but are roomy enough to allow the skier to manipulate straps on ski poles and boot bindings.

    Industry observers note that also consider breathability. If hands sweat and moisture collects inside the glove, it won’t matter that the shell is waterproof because hands will still get wet. Breathable gloves help some of the heat and moisture escape without letting in cold outer air and moisture.

    According to recent reports, now that you know a bit more about the factors to consider when choosing the best waterproof gloves for your needs, some questions may remain.     Waterproof means that absolutely no water makes its way into the glove. Water-resistant means that the gloves shed water to a degree before water comes in.

    #170207. What Actually Happens When Semi-Trucks Stop at Weigh Stations?

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Familyhandyman ↗ Open Full Page

    What Actually Happens When Semi-Trucks Stop at Weigh Stations?

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (555 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Familyhandyman

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that those roadside scales do more than weigh semitrucks.
    • Drivers pass truck weigh stations all the time, but few know everything these stations do or what happens when a truck pulls in.
    • Learn what happens when a truck pulls in, what inspectors look for, and why some drivers can keep going.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

    Recent findings suggest that those roadside scales do more than weigh semitrucks. Here’s what inspectors check and what happens when a truck pulls into a weigh station.

    Drivers pass truck weigh stations all the time, but few know everything these stations do or what happens when a truck pulls in. Once a semitruck exits and rejoins the highway, it’s hard to tell what goes on in between.

    Learn what happens when a truck pulls in, what inspectors look for, and why some drivers can keep going.

    Recent findings suggest that truck weigh stations help states enforce weight limits and spot safety problems. Trucks can weigh too much overall or carry too much weight on certain axles, putting extra strain on roads and bridges. On the Interstate System, the standard federal limits are 80,000 pounds gross vehicle weight, 20,000 pounds on a single axle, and 34,000 pounds on a tandem axle. Federal bridge weight rules and certain exceptions can also affect how much a truck may legally carry. Limits on other roads can vary.

    Rules vary by state. “Some require all commercial motor vehicles to stop, while others require only those above a certain weight to stop,” according to the Federal Highway Administration. “Ultimately, States must certify that they are enforcing their weight limits on certain highways in order not to jeopardize their receipt of Federal highway funds.”.

    Sources indicate that drivers who pull in follow signs directing them to a scale, where their trucks are weighed either while moving slowly or at a complete stop. If the weight is within the limits, they may be cleared to leave. Inspectors may still pull a truck aside for a closer look even when its weight is fine, based on screening results, visible defects, or random selection. An overweight truck may also be inspected further.

    Inspectors may check a truck’s tires, brakes, lights, and cargo, along with the driver’s records. They may also review credentials and permits, such as registration and fuel-tax paperwork, along with the driver’s hours-of-service logs. “There are eight levels of inspections ranging from the Level I Inspection, which evaluates both the driver and vehicle, to inspection levels with a more specific area of focus, such as Level VI for radioactive materials and Level VIII for electronic inspections,” according to the Commercial Vehicle Safety Alliance.

    Drivers of overweight trucks may receive a citation or have to move or remove some cargo before leaving. The exact consequences vary by state and violation.

    More serious safety problems, like faulty brakes, can put a truck or driver out of service. A truck placed out of service can’t return to the road until the problem is fixed. Drivers placed out of service must wait until their restrictions end.

    Industry observers note that some trucks can skip the stop altogether through electronic bypass programs. These programs use safety records and other information to determine whether a driver can continue without entering the station. Drivers still have to follow any signs or signals telling them to stop.

    Federal Highway Administration, “Questions and Answers About Vehicle Size and Weight” Federal Highway Administration, “Truck Size and Weight Enforcement Technologies, WIM Technology Overview” Federal Highway Administration, “Compliance Comparative Analysis Technical Report, Compliance Effectiveness of Enforcement” Commercial Vehicle Safety Alliance, “Inspections” Commercial Vehicle Safety Alliance, “Out-of-Service Criteria”.

    Crucial Snow Blower Maintenance Tasks to Complete Before the First Snow

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (772 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bobvila

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs.
    • In a recent development, imagine your frustration when your driveway is covered in snow after the first winter storm, but your snow blower won’t start.
    • By far the most important step is to make sure you have a fresh supply of fuel, says Dwyer.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

    In a recent development, imagine your frustration when your driveway is covered in snow after the first winter storm, but your snow blower won’t start. As winter approaches, it’s time to make sure your snow blower is ready to tackle that first snowfall. You’ll want to take a few steps to check that it’s tuned up and ready to go without a hitch. We spoke to Sean Dwyer, senior product manager for commercial and residential wheeled products at Husqvarna Group North America to identify the top snow blower maintenance tasks to prioritize so you are prepared when the first snowflake falls.

    By far the most important step is to make sure you have a fresh supply of fuel, says Dwyer. “If you have regular pump fuel, it should be less than 30 days old, and ideally premium grade that’s a non-ethanol blend,” he explains. Fuel can go stale over time and gum up the snow blower’s carburetor. Dwyer recommends running the unit out of gas before storing it. “Otherwise, at a minimum, purchase stabilized canned fuel or add a fuel stabilizer.” Gasoline with a stabilizer typically lasts for about 4 to 6 months.

    In a recent development, spend some time reviewing the key components of the unit. “This means checking engine oil and tire pressures, and also starting the unit to ensure proper wheel drive and auger operation,” notes Dwyer. “This is also a good time to shut the fuel off and run the carburetor dry to give your snow blower the best chance of a successful operation when you need it.”.

    In addition, pay attention to these additional parts of the snow blower:.

    Featuring an easy-to-pour package and effective formula, this motor oil washes dirt and deposits out of the engine as it passes through.

    Battery-powered snow blowers are convenient, but it’s crucial to recognize that cold weather and batteries don’t typically work well together, warns Dwyer. Checking battery health is part of regular snow blower maintenance. Rechargeable batteries can degrade over time, and won’t be able to hold as much charge as they age as they do when new. He recommends keeping fully charged batteries in the house or a location where they will remain above freezing temperatures. “If everything is in the cold garage, there is a good chance they won’t work when you need them to,” he explains. “Also, remember that when you are done, bring the batteries back to a warm place so they are ready to go next time.”.

    Snow blowers typically contain shear bolts (also called pins) as a safety feature. The shear bolts are designed to break to protect the auger gears from damage if the unit runs into hard objects like ice from a blizzard. There is typically one pin on each auger and one or two on the impeller.

    To change these components, wear protective gloves. “With the engine shut off, try to rotate each individual auger by hand,” claims Dwyer. “You should not be able to rotate the augers, and the shear bolts will be visually present.” To check the impeller, look for the shear bolts, or hold one of the augers firmly, and slowly try to turn the impeller. “Be careful when checking the impeller, as it is tied to the shaft that will drive the augers.”.

    It has been revealed that if these items spin freely, the shear bolt is likely damaged or missing, claims Dwyer. Replace any missing or broken bolts to protect your snow blower. It’s a good idea to always keep a stash of shear bolts on hand.

    Designed to wear down with use, skid shoes help keep a snow blower’s housing at the correct height and also protect your pavement. They are located on the lower sides of the auger housing and are designed to hold the scraper, located at the bottom of the auger housing, just above the ground, indicates Dwyer. “As these shoes wear, the scraper will contact the ground and wear will increase,” he explains.

    “A simple way to adjust the shoes is to sit the snow blower scraper on something around ¼ inch thick, like a paint stir stick, and then loosen the bolts holding the shoes to adjust them down to contact the ground and retighten,” suggests Dwyer.

    Sources indicate that “That open metal cage on the left is just decorative framing to make the building look sleek and balanced,” one Reddit user commented. “The left side of the restaurant has lower ceilings for storage, coolers, and the drive-thru lane, so they added that hollow steel frame on top to match the height of the main dining room on the right. There are no stairs or deck up there, just standard roof stuff and AC units hidden behind the wall.”.

    Another commenter agreed, saying, “It’s just an architectural design feature to give visual balance.”.

    Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

    GTA6 let's you take a break from a life of crime to make some much-needed home repairs on Jason and Lucia's house.

    Just in case your algorithm is different from mine, here’s some news: Grand Theft Auto 6 officially released today. After 13 years of waiting, fans of the open-world action-adventure video game series can finally dive into a upcoming, richly detailed and fully realized virtual world. Boot up the game, and you’ll find yourself faced with surprising realism, a world of crime, and the ability to do just about whatever you want. That’s right, even… DIY home improvement jobs?

    Yep, you’re reading that right. As part of its commitment to realism, GTA developer Rockstar Games has given players the ability to do some honest-to-goodness, roll-up-your-sleeves-and-get-to-work home improvement virtually.

    It has been revealed that and it’s not just a short cutscene where you see the house magically go from disrepair to fully fixed up. You, as the player, have to actually do the work, whether you’re drywalling, painting, or roofing. Luckily, it’s just a video game because the game is also set in a fictional version of Florida in the summer, which is probably one of the last places on earth you’d want to be stuck doing any sort of construction work.

    Let’s take a look at a few of the home improvement jobs done by GTA6‘s Jason Duval and see if his work meets Family Handyman’s standards.

    Sources indicate that with his lady friend Lucia on the way back from prison, Jason decides to fix up the place… including the unfinished framing in the center of his living room. Luckily, Jason knows how to hang drywall. The gameplay represents the job pretty accurately— Jason holds the drywall in place and screws it into the studs with an impact driver. We don’t get to see any taping or mudding, though. 7/10.

    Next, we’ll inspect whether Jason should perhaps prioritize a career as a painter over his life of crime. The painting section is also pretty accurate to the average DIY painting experience. Jason has to choose between three different color options before pouring the paint into a tray and using a roller to paint the wall. It’s pretty boring, which is honestly just like painting in real life — so bonus points for immersive realism. 8/10.

    Industry observers note that one of the first things Jason knows he has to fix before Lucia arrives is the massive hole in his roof that’s letting in a near-constant drip of rain. Luckily, like a lot of DIYers, he has some roofing experience, a cordless nail gun and a stack of shingles just lying around for some reason. Again, this section is pretty realistic. If gamers want the full Florida roofing experience, though, they’ll have to crank their heaters to maximum or perhaps play the game in a sauna. 6/10.

    In a recent development, look, I get it. The Grand Theft Auto series is about living out fantasies, providing gamers a sandbox where they can virtually experience the impossible.

    Recent findings suggest that but still… “House repairs complete” is a bridge too far. Ask any DIYer, and they will tell you no house is ever fully repaired. Pretending home improvement work could ever be finished is just not realistic and really took me out of the experience. 3/10.

    Recent findings suggest that overall, the game is cool. But to be honest, I’m not sure what the point is now that the house repairs are complete.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, I may not live in Ohio anymore, but there are some Ohio legal news stories I continue to follow. Here's one.

    Recent findings suggest that soon-to-be-former Rep. Max Miller (R-OH) sued his ex-wife, Emily Moreno (daughter of Ohio Senator Bernie Moreno), for defamation. Now that suit has been dismissed, and arguably in the worst way for Miller: The court concluded that the core underlying allegation is "substantially true.".

    Miller filed the suit after the Daily Mail published a story reporting that Miller "hurled a pot of boiling water" at Moreno during an argument, and later wrote a note apologizing for the incident. As the court notes, an audio recording (that Miller released somehow thinking it would exonerate him) confirms the core of the claim. From the opinion:.

    Recent findings suggest that an audio recording of the parties discussing the incident supports Defendant Moreno's contention of truth. Defendant Moreno confronted Plaintiff about pouring "bowling hot water on me." Although Plaintiff denies pouring hot water on her neck, he further admits the incident occurred. Plaintiff specifically stated "it was never done to hurt you with intent." Plaintiffs intent is irrelevant to the basic fact of whether the incident occurred, which addresses the element of falsity.

    Industry observers note that plaintiff maintains that the gist or sting of hurling a pot of boiling water is "categorically different" than the actions Plaintiff states actually occurred. It is Plaintiffs burden to support his claims with credible, admissible evidence. Plaintiff has not shown that the statement about dousing Defendant Moreno with boiling hot water are false. The imputation that Plaintiff poured or doused Defendant Moreno with hot water is substantially true.

    The court also noted the lack of any evidence that Moreno was responsible for the Daily Mail's publication of the claims.

    The court dismissed Miller's suit with prejudice and awarded costs and attorney fees. Additional litigation arising out of the Miller-Moreno divorce is pending, and it's always possible Miller will appeal. Moreno is not the first woman to accuse Miller of abuse.

    More background from the Washington Post here.

    Recent findings suggest that [Note: As initially posted, I referred to Miller as "Former Rep. Miller." Of course, he is not yet a former representative, as his term has not yet ended, so I have updated the post accordingly.

    General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Reason ↗ Open Full Page

    The First Amendment, University Investigations, and Anti-Israel Lawprof's Case Against Univ. of Kentucky

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1743 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that some excerpts from the longish decision Friday by Judge Benjamin Beaton (E.D.
    • This opinion addresses the latest chapter in the ongoing saga concerning Professor Ramsi Woodcock, his commentary regarding Israel and Palestine, and the University of Kentucky's investigation into whether he violated Title VI or the school's technology or conduct policies….
    • Earlier this month, this Court denied law professor Ramsi Woodcock's request to halt the University of Kentucky's ongoing investigation into several comments he made related to his views on the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and his 2025 "Petition for Military Action Against Israel." Woodcock's initial submissions had not persuasively shown that the investigation was retaliatory in its origin or chilling in its ongoing effect.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that some excerpts from the longish decision Friday by Judge Benjamin Beaton (E.D. Ky.) in Woodcock v. Capilouto:.

    This opinion addresses the latest chapter in the ongoing saga concerning Professor Ramsi Woodcock, his commentary regarding Israel and Palestine, and the University of Kentucky's investigation into whether he violated Title VI or the school's technology or conduct policies….

    Earlier this month, this Court denied law professor Ramsi Woodcock's request to halt the University of Kentucky's ongoing investigation into several comments he made related to his views on the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and his 2025 "Petition for Military Action Against Israel." Woodcock's initial submissions had not persuasively shown that the investigation was retaliatory in its origin or chilling in its ongoing effect.

    But the order set an evidentiary hearing two weeks later to address these fact-dependent questions and Woodcock's request for a preliminary injunction. The investigation—which had lasted more than a year and whose report was already overdue—could not "last forever" without threatening Woodcock's First Amendment rights. And the University of Kentucky's corresponding "reassignment" of Woodcock from teaching duties throughout the investigation was increasingly hard to justify, particularly given the absence of any articulated suspicion of classroom disruption….

    Then, one week after the TRO decision, the outside investigator's 134-page sealed (for now) report finally landed. {That report is provisionally under seal pending the resolution of a motion to seal, which will be referred to a Magistrate Judge.} ….

    It has been revealed that [Now], the Dean of the law school could decide whether to lift Woodcock's reassignment from teaching and restore him to the classroom for the spring semester. This could happen as late as mid-December, according to counsel, without prejudicing Woodcock's ability to teach…. [And] the University President could decide, based on the investigative report, whether (in his view) Woodcock violated any laws or policies….

    The report and Woodcock's response have been published by the Kentucky Lantern (McKenna Horsley); Woodcock reports that this is because they were publicly filed in a parallel state case. The court had this to say about Woodcock's request for a temporary injunction to block any findings by the University President:.

    Industry observers note that during previous hearings, this Court observed that Woodcock's effort to end his reassignment from teaching stood on firmer ground that his request to halt the investigation itself. That view rested largely on caselaw that contemplated speech-related investigations consistent with the First Amendment yet considered whether any attendant consequences of such investigations abridged those rights based on a retaliatory purpose, chilled speech, or both. {See generally, e.g., Sensabaugh v. Halliburton (6th Cir. 2019) (no adverse action based on "letter of guidance" and reprimand in the context of a "independent law firm" investigation involving "scores of documents and text messages" and "seventeen different witnesses"); Moore v. Garnand (9th Cir. 2023) ("[W]e never held that a retaliatory investigation alone could violate the First Amendment, as our holding rested on much more than just a retaliatory investigation[.]").} ….

    Woodcock insists that the First Amendment bars the President from spending "weeks poring over documents" unrelated to "any arguable policy violation." "Whatever the University decides about spring teaching, findings issued on the investigator's report would injure Woodcock irreparably on their own." To the extent that review entails an inquiry into his political beliefs, Woodcock contends, the process is illegitimate and should be enjoined immediately….

    [But] a substantial body of caselaw indicates that a speech-related investigation alone generally doesn't amount to retaliation or adverse action. {See, e.g., Churchill v. Univ. of Colorado at Boulder (Colo. App. 2010) ("Courts have concluded that investigations alone are not adverse employment actions."); Sensabaugh (6th Cir. 2019) (concluding no adverse action even when context included a "painstakin[g] investigation"); Couch v. Board. of Trustees of Memorial Hospital of Carbon County (10th Cir. 2009) (investigation didn't amount to adverse action supporting First Amendment retaliation); Benningfield v. City of Houston (5th Cir. 1998) ("Although a reprimand can constitute an adverse employment action, an investigation does not[.]"); Moore ("[W]e have never held that a retaliatory investigation alone could violate the First Amendment"); Bell v. Sheriff of Broward County 1375 (11th Cir. 2021) ("[D]eputy Bell's five-day suspension with pay pending an investigation into his conduct is not an adverse action."). But as emphasized in the Court's previous TRO opinion, the caselaw in this area is hardly uniform and uncertainty remains about how different circuits might approach each specific factual scenario. See, e.g., Holt v. Pennsylvania (3d Cir. 2017) ("Our Circuit has not considered whether the initiation of an internal investigation can constitute an 'adverse action' for purposes of a First Amendment retaliation claim, and our sister circuits are split on the matter.").} The collateral consequences of an investigation, by contrast, may create an intolerable chill that could warrant judicial intervention. See, e.g., Levin v. Harleston (2d Cir. 1992); White v. Lee (9th Cir. 2000). The First Amendment leaves at least some room for employers to investigate their employees for perceived misconduct, even when the alleged offenses relate to speech. Waters v. Churchill (1994) (plurality op.) ("Only [investigative] procedures outside the range" of reasonableness violate First Amendment despite investigation's "risk of erroneously punishing protected speech."); Gartenberg v. Cooper Union (S.D.N.Y. 2025) (even protected speech may be relevant to determining "whether actionable harassment occurred").

    According to recent reports, woodcock hasn't pointed to any precedent halting a school's investigation based only on its existence or the "brand" or "reputational harm" that it might produce. To the contrary, the two precedents on which he relies most heavily are easily distinguishable.

    Sweezy v. Latest Hampshire (1957), is a 70-year-old precedent concerning a state attorney general's investigation into a professor's affiliation with the Communist and Progressive Parties. It had little, if anything, to say about the operations, autonomy, or academic interests of a university. Contra, e.g., Regents of University of Michigan v. Ewing (1985).

    Recent findings suggest that fischer v. Thomas (6th Cir. 2022), likewise sits far afield from the context of university governance and academic speech. In that pre-enforcement challenge, the Sixth Circuit barred a state judicial commission from initiating formal proceedings against two judicial candidates after it "sen[t] vague and threatening letter to [the] candidates on the eve of election." The opinion didn't address whether an investigation or its concluding findings amounted to adverse action or retaliation….

    Recent findings suggest that fifth, even assuming Woodcock could establish a likelihood of success on the merits of his retaliation claim, to obtain a TRO he'd have to show irreparable harm and the balance of the equities relative to third parties and the public. Irreparable harm likely requires at least some showing of subjective chill as well; otherwise a court would be left to wonder why and "whether it needs to act now." ….

    The current record does precious little to "identify speech that [Woodcock] wishes to make in the future but for the threat of prosecution of that future speech." Despite boilerplate assertions that he'd otherwise say and write more about Israel and Palestine, it's hardly clear that this investigation has chilled Woodcock's speech at all. He points to a paper called "A Law and Economics Argument for Ending Israel" that he hasn't yet submitted to the law reviews; diminished posting on his blog, called "the Antizionist Legal Studies Movement;" and allegedly decreased Twitter activity. Yet Woodcock's social-media and listserv posting hasn't stopped altogether; during this investigation he has continued to post on X and the AALS online discussion groups, including about Israel; he has filed at least four lawsuits, several of which have been covered in the press; he maintains a webpage supplying information about and soliciting support for his speech and litigation. Without further evidence, the Court cannot conclude that Woodcock will be chilled over the next two weeks.

    Although the general tendency in the caselaw to treat First Amendment violations as irreparable harm cautions against assigning dispositive weight to this factor, the weakness of Woodcock's showing on the current record at least cuts against automatic or presumptive injunctive relief to ameliorate any purported self-censorship….

    The court also pointed to the university's own interest in speaking about Woodcock's speech:.

    In a recent development, [A]n injunction barring the President from reacting to the investigator's findings would—even on Woodcock's own terms—remedy one arguable free-speech violation with another. As any law professor knows, Justice Brandeis taught that the "remedy" for disfavored speech should ordinarily be more speech—not additional suppression. A college president, just like a law professor, may presumptively speak—privately or publicly—about a matter of public and professional interest such as this. Indeed, both have done so during this process.

    In a recent development, and President Capiluto's own speech rights aren't the only countervailing interests at matter. The University has its own governance interests in the orderly and prompt resolution of a high-profile pending investigation. See Ewing ("Academic freedom thrives not only on the independent and uninhibited exchange of ideas among teachers and students, … but also, and somewhat inconsistently, on autonomous decisionmaking by the academy itself."). "Without this ability to investigate, a public employer would be left without recourse and would lose its 'greater leeway in its dealings with citizen employees.'".

    Given these compounding considerations, the Court concluded that no temporary order revisiting the Court's prior orders and specifically restraining the President was warranted based on these allegations of objective chill (regarding Woodcock's likelihood of success on the merits), subjective chill (regarding any irreparable harm associated with Woodcock's speech pending the forthcoming presidential findings), or the public and third-party interest in an orderly and prompt conclusion to an academic investigation….

    This order, to be clear, does not resolve whether the University officials' past actions constituted retaliation in violation of the First Amendment—a distinct and retrospective question, for which damages and attorney fees under 42 U.S.C. §§ 1983 & 1988 are at least potentially available (though the Defendants of course disagree). While those historical facts are necessary to Woodcock's showing of likelihood of success on the merits, even if proved they are not sufficient to warrant a restraining order, which requires a showing of ongoing chilled speech.

    Nor does this order address the propriety of any discipline that Woodcock might eventually face. As described above, those questions haven't ripened and follow their own administrative process—one the Sixth Circuit specifically contemplated might alter the abstention analysis….

    #170191. The Quorum Clause Case

    📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1162 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Reason ↗ Open Full Page

    The Quorum Clause Case

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1162 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that in 2020, during the early days of the pandemic, the House of Representatives adopted a rule that would allow absent members to cast a vote by proxy.
    • At the 2023 State of the Union Address in March 2023, every every seat was filled.
    • Don't tell me there was some actual need to bypass the quorum rule at this point.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that in 2020, during the early days of the pandemic, the House of Representatives adopted a rule that would allow absent members to cast a vote by proxy. At the time, there were ample warnings that this process had constitutional infirmities, but the House pressed ahead. Indeed, the House of Representatives continued to use the proxy rule through the end of 2022. One such bill was the Consolidation Appropriations Act of 2023. At this time, the justification for social distancing had passed. The upcoming House assembled in January 2023. I see no masks. Members of Congress are walking around with their families.

    At the 2023 State of the Union Address in March 2023, every every seat was filled. Look at this picture. I don't see many members wearing masks.

    Don't tell me there was some actual need to bypass the quorum rule at this point.

    Recent findings suggest that the pandemic was only a few years ago, but it is crucial to remember how many brazen violations of the Constitution there were in short order. As Justice Gorsuch wrote in Roman Catholic Diocese v. Brooklyn v. Cuomo, "Even if the Constitution has taken a holiday during this pandemic, it cannot become a sabbatical." The proxy rule was one such sabbatical.

    Industry observers note that in 2023, Texas challenged the constitutionality of one provision of the appropriations bill, the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act. In 2024, Judge Hendrix of the Northern District of Texas wrote a magisterial opinion that stretched more than one-hundred pages. He explained in depth why the enrolled bill doctrine does not block review and why the proxy rule violates the quorum clause. At the time, I read the opinion and thought Judge Hendrix put forward an extremely justification. The House tried to take a shortcut and got caught. A panel of the Fifth Circuit reversed, but now the en banc Fifth Circuit has affirmed Judge Hendrix's decision.

    I'll admit, the immediate reaction to this decision is "it can't be right!" This intuition, I submit, is based more on the consequences than the merits. If every bill passed during the COVID period is now subject to a constitutional challenge, the consequences could be serious. But I encourage you to back off the consequentialism. Far too many judges and lawyers start with the consequences and work their way backwards. If the House of Representatives decided to take a shortcut and ignored a constitutional requirement, then the members of that body should bear the consequences of their decision.

    Recent findings suggest that the en banc Fifth Circuit split (as if often does) by a 9-8 vote. Thankfully, there were no senior judges on the three-judge panel. Judge Wilson wrote the majority opinion and Judge Graves wrote the dissent. Judge Haynes continues her unusual practice where she doesn't join any opinion, reducing her thoughts to a single footnote.

    * Judge Haynes states that she does not think it is appropriate to throw out the Federal House of Representatives in this arena, so she dissents. She also appreciates Judge Graves's dissent.

    Judge Haynes might think she is being clever, but I doubt anyone else agrees. Indeed, in a number of recent cases, Judge Haynes simply writes that she affirms for the reasons stated by the district court--as if nothing that her colleagues wrote made a difference. I think it demonstrates a lack of respect to her colleagues who spend considerable time preparing opinions and she doesn't even bother explaining where she disagrees. She is capable of writing reasoned opinions, but just shrugs at the en banc stage.

    In a recent development, judges Wilson and Judge Graves agree that Texas has standing. They further agree that the enrolled bill rule does not preclude review. The disagreement is purely a legal question about whether the proxy rule violates the Quorum Clause. Having read both the majority and dissenting opinions, I don't think the problem is even close. The strongest argument for the dissent is the "Unanimous Consent" rule, and the majority demolishes that argument.

    In a recent development, what happens next? It's complicated.

    I am fairly certain that the new Attorney General opposes this case and will do everything in his power to scuttle the suit, as well as the Fifth Circuit's en banc precedent. In recent days, the Texas Attorney General has been dismissing and settling many cases. The reason, I suspect, is to avoid giving the new Attorney General a vehicle to enter into binding consent decrees. I suppose it is conceivable that Texas will try to enter into some kind of settlement with the United States. Or maybe Texas just moves to dismiss the case with prejudice before January 1. That would end the case, but leave the Fifth Circuit's precedent in place.

    In a recent development, I suppose another state with a similar Article III injury could intervene. I am not certain about the timing as there is a final judgment in place--although a judgment is not really final until a cert petition is disposed of.

    If this case stays alive past January, the United States will almost certainly file a cert petition. The fresh Texas Attorney General will not oppose certiorari and may ask for a summary reversal. I suspect the new AG could even argue that since there is no adversity, there is no longer a live Article III case, and the Fifth Circuit decision should be vacated under Musingwear. I am not entirely sure how Munsingwear applies when the Attorney General switches sides, but we may soon find out. Then again, the Supreme Court routinely decides cases in which there is no adversity, so the case might continue.

    Indeed, the Supreme Court might also think it prudent to settle this matter. These challenges can arise in other contexts, and the longer this issue festers, the worse it will be. If so, the Court could appoint an amicus to defend the Fifth Circuit's judgment.

    Recent findings suggest that at that point, what will happen? Again, all members of the Fifth Circuit agreed that Texas has standing and the enrolled bill rule doesn't bar review. I suppose the Supreme Court could reject those holdings, but that would be rather transparent.

    According to recent reports, once you get to the merits, the Court will have to do some work. I've seen some commentators lead of with a discussion of how many laws might be at risk. One of those statutes is the Electoral Count Reform Act of 2022. I'll close where I started. The meaning of the Constitution should not change based on the consequences. Either the House had a quorum or it didn't.

    In a recent development, do I have faith that a majority of the Supreme Court will follow that original meaning of the Constitution? No, I don't. Maybe three votes, at the most--which is often how the Fifth Circuit fares. But don't pretend the Supreme Court is making its ruling based on law.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs.
    • While it’s convenient to treat your garage as an all-purpose storage area, plummeting temperatures can ruin valuable gear and create serious safety risks for your family.
    • In a recent development, avoid storing perishable food and canned goods in the garage.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

    While it’s convenient to treat your garage as an all-purpose storage area, plummeting temperatures can ruin valuable gear and create serious safety risks for your family. Before it gets too cold outside, you’ll want to remove certain items from your unheated garage and find a more appropriate storage space. We asked professional organizer Lori Bailey, founder and owner of Miss Organized in the New York/New Jersey area, about the most common household goods that are typically stored in a garage but shouldn’t be, and where to keep them instead.

    In a recent development, avoid storing perishable food and canned goods in the garage. This includes rice, beans, soup, dried fruit, nuts, cereal, pasta, canned and bottled drinks, and even pet food. “I will often see people use their garages as an extension of their pantry, especially when they buy in bulk,” states Bailey. “However, canned foods should not be exposed to freezing temperatures since that can compromise the seal and safety of the food.” This can result in bacteria entering and spoiling the food.

    It has been revealed that cans also can burst, or the food itself could actually freeze, which can ruin its taste and texture. In addition, food that comes in cardboard packaging is vulnerable to pests like rodents and insects. “Your pantry, kitchen cabinets, or a storage room in the basement are much better options for your food,” advises Bailey.

    According to recent reports, paint is one of the most common items that Bailey sees stored in garages, but extreme cold can actually ruin it. “When paint freezes, it can separate and become lumpy, making it unusable.” Some paint can even get ruined before your thermometer drops to 32 degrees Fahrenheit; latex paint, for example, should be stored in a place that doesn’t drop below 50 degrees Fahrenheit. Chemicals such as cleaners, solvents, and automotive fluids also can spoil, leak, or even become a fire hazard if stored in an unheated garage during winter. Bring these products inside and store them in a well-ventilated and temperature-controlled area, such as a basement utility room, laundry room, or storage closet, says Bailey.

    Industry observers note that critical paperwork like passports and birth certificates, photographs, children’s artwork, and sentimental keepsakes should never be stored in an unheated garage, indicates Bailey. “I always tell my clients that paper clutter needs a proper home since moisture and temperature fluctuations can cause paper to warp, photographs to stick together, and sentimental items to deteriorate.” Rodents can also get in and destroy papers. Bailey recommends keeping these items in labeled, protective containers inside your home.

    With a heat resistance of up to 5,200 degrees Fahrenheit and a lock, this storage bag offers exceptional protection for your valuable documents.

    Leaving sensitive electronics, battery-operated devices, and batteries in an unheated garage over the winter can also be problematic, permanently ruining their internal components and drastically shortening their lifespan. This includes everything from standard household batteries to rechargeable power tool batteries and lawn mower batteries. Temperature swings can cause delicate microchips and circuitry to expand and contract, as well as condensation that can lead to rust and corrosion. To protect your gear and maintain peak performance, relocate all electronic devices and remove batteries from your tools before the first freeze, storing them in a dry, temperature-controlled area of your home.

    Bailey also sees many people storing holiday decorations in their garages. However, some of those items, even if placed in bins, can’t withstand freezing temperatures. “Candles can crack or warp, and certain decorative materials, adhesives, and finishes can deteriorate,” warns Bailey. “I always encourage my clients to be selective about what goes into seasonal storage and to keep temperature-sensitive decorations indoors.”.

    • Industry observers note that typically a summer bloomer, jasmine can bloom during the winter, adding sweet fragrance to indoor spaces.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

    According to recent reports, winter is a long season of brown lawns, bare trees, and frost-covered shrubs. Our feeling is that if we can’t get color and cheer in outdoor beds this time of year, we may as well cultivate some color indoors. Poinsettias are common, colorful blooms for this season, but aren’t for everyone because they’re toxic to pets, according to the ASPCA. But who says your wintertime plant picks have to be Christmas-themed, or even red? Try these cheerful houseplants on for size, or gift them to your nearest and dearest this season.

    Industry observers note that typically a summer bloomer, jasmine can bloom during the winter, adding sweet fragrance to indoor spaces. To encourage rebloom the following year, give it a time-out in the fall in a room that is completely dark at night. Exposure to street light or indoor lighting will interrupt the cycle. Give this nontoxic plant a trim once it blooms, since jasmine tends to get leggy.

    From December to April, cyclamen, which can bloom for weeks, sends up lightly fragrant flowers above heart-shaped, silver-marbled foliage. After flowering, the plant loses its leaves and dies back for the summer. Some owners might be tempted to toss spent cyclamens into the trash, but take note: The plant is not dead, just dormant. Continue to water it once in a while and when temperatures cool, it will start growing again. Cyclamen is toxic and should be kept away from cats, dogs, and kids.

    These striking succulent houseplants have been popular holiday gifts since the 1800s.     Recent findings suggest that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

    Homeowners with boxelder trees (a type of maple tree that produces seed-bearing pods) may be all too familiar with the bugs that tend to follow. Boxelder bugs, named for their preferred host, are ½-inch-long black insects with red or orange markings along their wings. They feed on seeds and leaves from boxelders and a few other trees like ash and maple, but they don’t cause serious damage to plants, homes, or humans. Still, when these bugs gather in large numbers, they become a major nuisance—especially when they invade homes and release their distinctive, musty smell.

    In fall, boxelder bugs migrate toward warmth, often swarming on the south- and west-facing walls of homes, garages, sheds, and trees. If they find small cracks or gaps, they’ll slip inside to overwinter in walls, attics, or basements—sometimes appearing indoors on sunny winter days. Even homes without box elder trees nearby aren’t entirely safe: These bugs are highly attracted to warmth and light-colored siding, making them a common seasonal pest in many regions.

    If you’re tired of seeing these bugs on your siding—or worse, inside your house—take charge now with these smart strategies for getting rid of boxelder bugs.

    It has been revealed that boxelder bugs (Boisea trivittata) are easy to recognize once you know what to look for. Adult bugs are about ½ inch long, with black bodies and reddish-orange markings along their wings and thorax. Their long, oval shape and bold color contrast make them easy to spot—especially when they gather in large groups on sunny walls or trees.

    Juvenile boxelder bugs, known as nymphs, are smaller and bright red with no wings, though they develop darker coloration and wing pads as they mature. You’ll typically see these bugs in late summer and fall, when both adults and nymphs are most active.

    Despite their intimidating appearance, boxelder bugs are harmless to people, pets, and homes. They don’t bite or sting, and they won’t eat through drywall, wood, or furniture. However, their tendency to swarm in large numbers—and release a pungent odor when crushed—makes them a frustrating nuisance pest, especially when they get indoors.

    Boxelder bugs are often mistaken for other insects, like stink bugs or milkweed bugs. What sets them apart is their distinctive red-lined wings, flattened body, and preference for warm, sunlit surfaces. If you notice clusters of bugs on the south or west sides of your home, windows, or trees in fall, you’re likely dealing with boxelder bugs.

    Boxelder bugs follow a predictable seasonal pattern, which explains why they seem to appear all at once. In spring, adults emerge from their overwintering spots—usually inside walls or attics—and head outdoors to feed and lay eggs on box elder, maple, and ash trees.

    By summer, the eggs hatch into bright red nymphs, which mature into winged adults by late summer. These adults become most visible in fall, when they gather in large numbers on sunlit walls and tree trunks, especially on the south and west sides of homes.

    Sources indicate that as temperatures drop, they look for cracks and gaps in buildings to overwinter indoors. Though mostly dormant through winter, they may occasionally reappear on warm, sunny days—often near windows or light sources.

    Knowing their seasonal behavior makes it easier to time prevention efforts, especially in early fall when they begin looking for a way inside.

    Sources indicate that if the bugs are in your house, don’t panic—they won’t bite, sting, or reproduce inside. Still, their smell and stains can be unpleasant. Use these simple methods to get them out and keep them from coming back.

    Boxelder bugs slip in through small cracks around windows, doors, vents, and siding.

    In a recent development, do this in early fall before they try to move in for winter. Once they’re inside, they’re much harder to control.

    Boxelder bugs often hide in basements, attics, or ceiling corners, especially during colder months. To catch the sneaky ones, set up glue or light-based traps in these low-traffic areas.

    According to recent reports, replace traps regularly to avoid lingering odors. While traps won’t eliminate a boxelder bug infestation, they’re a great supplemental tool for catching stragglers inside the home.

    For quick, chemical-free control, just vacuum up any boxelder bugs you find on floors, windowsills, or walls.

    In a recent development, boxelder bugs don’t reproduce indoors. Once you’ve cleared them out and sealed up entry points, they shouldn’t come back.

    Instead of reaching for harsh chemical pesticides (they’re not very helpful here), mix up a DIY soap spray to kill boxelder bugs on contact.

    Boxelder bugs are most active outdoors in late summer and fall, especially around sunny walls, tree trunks, and light-colored siding. Taking action early can reduce the number trying to get indoors.

    If you spot small groups of boxelder bugs gathering on your home’s siding, foundation, or trees, a strong blast from a garden hose can break them up.

    Reducing their numbers outside can help you avoid a full-blown infestation indoors later on.

    For larger swarms, diatomaceous earth is a natural and pet-safe way to kill boxelder bugs outdoors.

    Recent findings suggest that this fine powder pierces the bugs’ exoskeletons, causing them to dry out and die within hours. Reapply diatomaceous earth after it rains, or if the bugs return.

    In general, chemical sprays are not the first recommendation for managing boxelder bugs. Experts at the University of California Integrated Pest Management program advise that insecticide sprays are often no more effective than vacuuming or using a garden hose, and require repeated application for limited results.

    Sources indicate that however, if bugs are clustered on the exterior of your house and you’ve already tried sealing, trapping, vacuuming, and all of these other recommendations, a professional-grade perimeter spray may help. For persistent infestations in late summer or early fall, a licensed pest professional may apply EPA-approved synthetic pyrethroid insecticides (like deltamethrin, bifenthrin, cyfluthrin, or permethrin) to the foundation, siding seams, eaves, window and door trim, and attic vents to create a residual barrier.

    Industry observers note that since the pests feed on the seedpods of female box elder trees, removing them and replacing them with non-seed-bearing male trees (or other species) can help you get rid of the bugs permanently. Keep in mind that the more mature the tree, the costlier it will be to remove. Also, consider that the benefits of the tree—shade, privacy, and curb appeal—may outweigh the insect nuisance.

    Warm fall weather and nearby box elder, maple, or ash trees attract the bugs to sunlit walls and cracks.

    Remove seed-bearing trees, seal entry points, clean up debris, and use non-chemical control methods.

    Sources indicate that there’s no proven scent that reliably repels them, despite some anecdotal claims. You’re usually better off using a light trap or a hose to spray them away.

    No—vinegar may deter them briefly, but it doesn’t kill them.

    Yes, if DIY methods fail or infestations are large and persistent, call in the pros.

    According to recent reports, professor John Yoo is leaving the law school at the University of California at Berkeley to join the School of Civic Leadership at the University of Texas at Austin.     Given the attention his move has received, Yoo has written an op-ed for the New York Post explaining his decision to choose Texas, and disputing any suggestion that he was driven out of Berkeley.

    I'm leaving not because I feel driven out by Berkeley — anything but.

    In my three decades there I've enjoyed working, on an individual level, with spirited, ambitious students and challenging, innovative scholars.

    I'm moving because Berkeley, like its peers, has declined from a daring, risk-taking center of higher learning to one that wallows contentedly in a monoculture of liberalism.

    Yoo claims the school has been obsessed with ethnic diversity while disregarding viewpoint diversity, and that this has eroded the institution's commitment to free speech and created an environment in which anti-semitism has taken root.

    I've watched students and the usual agitators disrupt debates on affirmative action, spark pitched fights on Sproul Plaza and try to shout down distinguished scholars and thinkers (home of the Free Speech Movement, indeed).

    Tolerance of such shenanigans was matched by intolerance of conservative or libertarian views on the faculty.

    It has been revealed that berkeley has consistently rejected conservative scholars, no matter how well-qualified, well-published or widely cited. . . .

    Second Amendment Roundup: AR-15 Film Redux.

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (782 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that last week, Professor Mark W.
    • That federal judges are now reviewing Internet videos to learn about firearms is hardly surprising.
    • As I previously wrote, I had the pleasure of introducing the "AR-15 Primer" film.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that last week, Professor Mark W. Smith released his latest 85-minute film discussing the operations and mechanics of modern firearms, including semiautomatic rifles such as the popular AR-15 rifle. The film, titled "Firearms and the AR-15 Rifle: A Primer for the Bench and Bar," can be found on YouTube here and on Rumble. It has already been viewed over 23,000 times since its release only days ago. The film is broken down into 25 segments so a viewer can jump from topic to topic.

    That federal judges are now reviewing Internet videos to learn about firearms is hardly surprising. A few weeks ago Judge Doris Pryor of the Seventh Circuit made reference to this during oral argument in a constitutional fight over the legality of Illinois's suppressor ban. In the consolidated cases of Anderson v. Raoul and Morse v. Raoul, argued October 28, 2026, she acknowledged that she has watched videos in preparing for oral argument. The oral argument audio recording is here with Judge Pryor's comment at the 25:04-25:23 mark.

    As I previously wrote, I had the pleasure of introducing the "AR-15 Primer" film. From there, Rick Vasquez (a former ATF firearm technician and U.S. Marine ordnance officer) takes the spotlight explaining the mechanical operation of today's AR-15 rifle and its typical features.

    Sources indicate that but there is another crucial aspect of the film that is worth noting. And that is the impressive animations found within the film that help educate legal professionals and the general public about the internal and related operations of the AR-15 (and most modern semi-automatic rifles).

    According to recent reports, the animations found throughout the film are informative for those learning about firearm mechanics. Here are a few of the noteworthy ones:.

    In a recent development, there is an excellent 2-minute animation illustrating how gas-operated semiautomatic rifles internally deploy the rapidly-expanding gases from the firing of a shot to do two things: first, to send a projectile (the bullet) down the barrel and, second, to prepare the rifle to fire the next round of ammunition. This is called autoloading. This dual use of the gases from firing a single shot is generally not understood or appreciated by those upcoming to firearms technology, but the film's animation makes it clear. This animation also clarifies that autoloading does not mean automatic fire (like one sees with a M16 machine gun). The animation can be seen at the 14:58 to 17:58 mark of the film.

    Industry observers note that the film also does a nice job demonstrating the physical reality of recoil by illustrating how the features of an AR-15 like the straight line stock, the buffer spring/buffer tube, and the muzzle brake help to minimize recoil allowing for a more comfortable and effective shooting experience. The 28:09 to 28:22 mark has a nice illustration of the straight-line stock while the 28:28 to 28:59 mark illustrates the role of the buffer and buffer spring in minimizing uncomfortable recoil. The 27:59 to 28:07 mark reveals an animation illustrating what constitutes recoil from the firing of a rifle.

    Industry observers note that the film also effectively uses animation to illustrate the difference between scopes, red dot optics, and iron sights. A scope magnifies the target making it appear closer than it really is; a red dot optic helps the user aim the rifle using an electronic dot without magnification; and iron sights entail aligning a front post with a rear sight. The 1:00:53 to 1:01:18 mark illustrates these differences.

    Sources indicate that animation also helps viewers understand that the barrel of a semiautomatic rifle gets hot when the rifle is fired due to the internal gas explosion that results from firing a round. The film's animation demonstrates the rifle barrel heating up and demonstrates the value of handguards (often called "barrel shrouds" in legislation) to protect the user of the rifle. The 46:24 to 46:33 mark illustrates a barrel heating up as the rifle is shot.

    The film's use of animations to explain the difference between a bullet and a cartridge is also worth mentioning. Lawyers (and even some judges) use those terms interchangeably, but they mean very different things. The 1:10:12 to 1:11:08 mark illustrates the four components (primer, gun power, case and bullet) of a modern ammunition cartridge.

    It has been stated that the late President Harry Truman embraced the thought, "I am from Missouri so you have to show me." Well, Professor Smith's upcoming film on firearm mechanics works hard to "show" (through animations, illustrations and images) the internal mechanics and features of AR-15 semiautomatic rifles. And I suspect the bench and the bar will be the better for it.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Nicolas Tiangaye, a prominent Central African lawyer, human rights defender, and former prime minister died in Bangui on November 16, at the age of 70.
    • Industry observers note that tiangaye first came into the spotlight as a young lawyer when he defended the former emperor, Jean-Bédel Bokassa, in 1986.
    • For Tiangaye, the cardinal rule that all defendants must benefit from their right to a fair trial is one he lived by.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Nicolas Tiangaye, a prominent Central African lawyer, human rights defender, and former prime minister died in Bangui on November 16, at the age of 70. One of the country's most respected rule of law advocates, his career spanned more than four decades.

    Industry observers note that tiangaye first came into the spotlight as a young lawyer when he defended the former emperor, Jean-Bédel Bokassa, in 1986. Later he defended the future president, François Bozizé, when he was accused of plotting a coup.

    For Tiangaye, the cardinal rule that all defendants must benefit from their right to a fair trial is one he lived by. By the early 1990s, Tiangaye was one of the leading Central African human rights advocates and served as the Bar Association president.

    In 1996 he was the lead defense council for Jean-Paul Akayesu before the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda. Human Rights Watch strongly advocated for the prosecution of Akayesu hailing his 1998 conviction as a historic international precedent. I once discussed the seminal conviction with Tiangaye and he reiterated that a good lawyer must be willing to defend clients and insist on due process, even in highly charged circumstances.

    Sources indicate that throughout the 1990s and 2000s, he spoke out for judicial independence and democratic governance. This often put him at odds with the government. But threats, he said, came with the job.

    He regularly ended up at the heart of national politics. Following Bozizé's successful coup, Tiangaye helped draft the 2004 Constitution. In January 2013, then-president Bozizé appointed Tiangaye prime minister amidst national turmoil. He remained in the position after Seleka seized Bangui and committed widespread abuses. Tiangaye despised the Seleka’s crimes, he told me, and he resigned.

    Recent findings suggest that he returned to legal practice and his passion: defending the Constitution. He became an outspoken critic of President Faustin-Archange Touadéra's efforts to remove presidential term limits, insisting on constitutional safeguards and political pluralism.

    In a recent development, his death is both a professional and personal loss for Human Rights Watch. More importantly, it occurs as independent voices and institutions remain under pressure in the Central African Republic. I spoke with him just last week about detained activists. I wish I asked how he would like to be remembered. I imagine he would have insisted that we not focus on the individual, but on his commitment to the rule of law and human rights—Tiangaye’s ultimate legacy.

    US Expulsions of Third-Country Nationals to Countries in Africa.

There are important disputes tied to climate change, immigration, and the Second Amendment. But no case is quite comparable to last term’s battles over tariffs, birthright citizenship, executive authority, and the Voting Rights Act.
