    My forthcoming chapter on "Emergency Powers" is now available on SSRN. It is coauthored with Josh Braver (University of Wisconsin), and will be published in the forthcoming Cato Handbook on Executive Power, edited by Molly Nixon. Braver is a leading expert on the law of domestic use of the military and a liberal/progressive. I am a a libertarian. If we can come to agreement on these challenges, I hope others can, as well. Here is the abstract:.

    Emergency powers are special types of government authorities that are only supposed to be used under extraordinary circumstances, in order to address a crisis. But, over time, many have become institutionalized as near-blank checks that the executive can invoke at will. This situation imperils civil liberties and our constitutional system.

    According to recent reports, this chapter goes over the major US emergency powers, including the National Emergencies Act, the Insurrection Act, the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), and others, and offers proposals for curbing the dangers they create. Effective reform requires a combination of newly introduced legislation and strong, nondeferential judicial review.

    I recently covered related problems in an article for Just Security, which goes over potential legislative reforms. In the Cato Handbook chapter, Braver and I cover both legislative reforms and how judicial review can be strengthened.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Since early November, many rural communities in the Catatumbo region, near the Colombia-Venezuela border, have suffered violent abuses and forced displacement as the 33rd Front, a dissident group of the former Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), has clashed with the National Liberation Army (ELN) over control of the territory.

    During a field visit from November 9 to 12, Human Rights Watch interviewed community members, representatives of civil society organizations, humanitarian workers, and local authorities, who remarked these groups have continued to kill civilians, recruit children, plant antipersonnel mines, carry out drone attacks, and impose strict social control over communities.

    People told us that on November 8 in Caño Salado, a rural community in Tibú, members of the 33rd Front threatened residents and accused them of collaborating with the ELN. Two community leaders were killed. “They told people to leave, or they would kill anyone who was involved with the ELN,” a civil society member told Human Rights Watch.

    Dozens of families have also been displaced from Bocas de San Miguel and El Diamante, according to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs.

    According to media reports, armed groups have also carried out six attacks using drones armed with explosives in Catatumbo in the first half of November, killing at least five people, including one civilian, and injuring 14 civilians.

    The situation in Catatumbo has been critical since early 2025, when Human Rights Watch documented that armed groups killed, assaulted, kidnapped, disappeared civilians and caused the displacement of more than 100,000 people.

    According to official announcements, since President De la Espriella took office in August, the government has carried out three airstrikes in Catatumbo, resulting in 10 deaths. The strikes were followed by Colombian army ground operations that resulted in six arrests, and the recovery of two children who had been recruited by armed groups. Community members told us these actions have done little to reduce armed groups’ violence and control over communities.

    The government should urgently protect civilians, by ensuring that its security strategy goes beyond military operations. It should include effective law enforcement and criminal prosecutions, a stronger humanitarian response, support for affected communities, and targeted social and economic policies to reduce the high levels of poverty that fuel the strength of armed groups in the region.

    #170126. Listening to the past

    Listening to the past

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1848 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Originalism sometimes requires judges to sift a historical record to determine what the law is.
    • In a column last year, I considered a common criticism of originalism: that judges make poor historians.
    • In a recent development, A related criticism of originalism is that history makes a poor judge.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Originalism sometimes requires judges to sift a historical record to determine what the law is. That is because it holds that we should give the Constitution its original meaning, and the text of the Constitution does not always make that meaning readily apparent to modern readers.

    In a column last year, I considered a common criticism of originalism: that judges make poor historians. Maybe, I concluded, but they can still be good (originalist) judges.

    In a recent development, A related criticism of originalism is that history makes a poor judge. Judges must be decisive, but historical inquiry is often inconclusive. This month’s column considers this criticism – specifically, two common forms that it takes: (1) originalism attributes too much significance to historical silence, and (2) originalism cannot reconcile dissonant historical traditions.

    The role of history in text-and-history cases.

    In a recent development, originalists turn to the historical record for a variety of purposes. Because originalism holds that the Constitution means today what it meant in 1789 (except to the extent that it has been lawfully amended), understanding the meaning of its words requires looking to historical sources to figure out how those words were used at the time the Constitution was ratified. To take an uncontroversial example, while a modern reader might read “domestic violence” and think “spousal abuse,” historical context reveals that “domestic Violence” in the guarantee clause means internal civil unrest.

    Recent findings suggest that sometimes, however, originalists look to the historical record for purposes other than uncovering the contemporary definition of the Constitution’s words. Sometimes, it is necessary to look to history to understand what those words did, legally speaking.

    It has been revealed that for example, it is relatively easy to understand the opening words of Article III: “The judicial Power of the United States, shall be vested in one supreme Court, and in such inferior Courts as the Congress may from time to time ordain and establish.” But what is the significance of the decision to give the “judicial Power of the United States” to Article III courts and not, say, to “the executive Departments”? The answer to that question is not to be found exclusively in a dictionary definition of “judicial Power.” It is to be found in historical sources revealing what, in 1789, the “judicial Power” enabled an actor to do. Whatever that is, Article III courts can do it, and an executive department cannot.

    Recent findings suggest that similarly, the Second Amendment guarantees that “the right of the people to keep and bear Arms, shall not be infringed.” But we know that that right has always been understood to coexist with some limited forms of regulation. We will not necessarily be able to figure out what forms of regulation are permissible just by looking at how “right” and “infringed” were used in old dictionaries. Courts must uncover a more complex historical idea.

    Industry observers note that that is why 2022’s Fresh York State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n v. Bruen, an originalist opinion in which the court held that New York’s concealed carry law was inconsistent with the Second Amendment, requires courts adjudicating Second Amendment challenges to move past the text to look at history: namely, “the Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation.” If the government can prove that its firearms regulation fits the history, then the government may prevail even though it seeks to restrict the right described in the text.

    One consequence of the Bruen methodology is that, if the government cannot find a historical regulation that resembles its modern regulation, then it may lose. This is a problem, critics argue, because there are plenty of reasons the legislatures of the past might have chosen not to regulate in a particular way.

    According to recent reports, for example, the founding generation did not disarm casual users of intoxicating substances. One reason may be that they believed such a regulation would infringe the right to keep and bear arms. An early refusal to regulate on that ground would then provide good evidence that the right was originally understood to foreclose the would-be regulation. But there are other possibilities: the regulation would have been inexpedient, impolitic, unnecessary. Or perhaps it just never occurred to the legislators.

    If the government cannot fit its modern regulation into the historical regulatory tradition, then the modern regulation fails Bruen’s test. Thus, Bruen does not distinguish these sources of silence. It seems to draw the same inference from them: unconstitutionality.

    This criticism – that the lack of a historical regulatory tradition doesn’t tell you very much – is misplaced for several reasons. First, historical legislatures legislated against a background common-law tradition that included robust principles concerning appropriate firearm regulation, even if those principles weren’t spelled out in legislation. The common-law practices on which the court relied in, say, United States v. Rahimi (in which it upheld a federal law disarming persons under a domestic violence restraining order) are part of that tradition and reveal a baseline principle: the state may act on demonstrated or threatened misuse of firearms by individuals. Legislative silence was not regulatory silence – the common law hummed on.

    Second, and relatedly, courts do not treat historical regulations as “molds” into which modern legislators must pour their regulatory ambitions. Rather, as Justice Amy Coney Barrett explained in her concurrence in Rahimi, the historical inquiry “demands a wider lens: Historical regulations reveal a principle, not a mold.” Principles convert some silences into spaces for modern regulatory innovation: firearms laws that differ in detail, but not in principle, from their predecessors. Conversely, if no historical regulation anywhere, anytime reflects the principle animating a restriction on someone’s ability to keep and bear arms (as was the case in last term’s decision rejecting a federal attempt to disarm someone based on casual drug use in United States v. Hemani), then that “silence” speaks more eloquently than originalism’s critics imagine.

    Finally, and most key in my view, the criticism mistakes the role of the historical inquiry in Second Amendment adjudications. The text of the Second Amendment is the first and best evidence of its meaning, and it is always speaking. Bruen directs courts to begin with the text and turn to history only after concluding that the regulation implicates the Second Amendment. Before a court ever turns to the “historical tradition of firearm regulation,” then, it has already concluded that the government is restricting someone’s ability to keep and bear arms. To the extent that silences in the historical record create doubt about whether that restriction is permissible or impermissible, the textual analysis justifies shifting the burden of that uncertainty onto the government. The government has failed to justify restricting what the Constitution describes as protected conduct. Tie goes to the rights-holder.

    According to recent reports, sometimes, judges face the opposite problem: not silence, but too much noise. Professor Rachel Bayefsky wrote last week about seemingly dissonant traditions at play in Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards, a case in which the court heard argument on Nov. 10.

    Sun Valley involves an appeal from a Department of Labor enforcement action imposing penalties on Sun Valley Orchards for breaching work contracts with foreign laborers brought into the country under the H-2A visa program. The court must decide whether that enforcement action, which the department both prosecuted and adjudicated, belongs instead in an Article III court.

    Recent findings suggest that recall that only Article III courts hold “the judicial Power of the United States.” History reveals that the government needs the “judicial Power” to deprive someone – like Sun Valley Orchards – of a private right, like property. But it does not need to exercise judicial power to exercise a sovereign (or so-called “public”) right, like the right to decide who enters the country, or to confer a privilege, like a visa. To put it a little more simply: If the government wants to take money that is already in your bank account, then it must take you to court. If you want the government to pay you money that is in the Treasury, then the government can handle your request “in house” (i.e., in the agency charged with administering the benefits scheme).

    It has been revealed that bayefsky describes these as competing traditions brought into conflict by the parties’ claims: Sun Valley invokes its private right to the money the department seeks to collect from it; the department brandishes its sovereign power and the conditions it attached to the privilege of hiring foreign laborers. Bayefsky suggests that the conflict creates an indeterminacy, which the court might resolve by turning to considerations other than text and history to reach a conclusion about what the Constitution requires today.

    Many voices, like silences, present a challenge to originalism. But varied traditions do not foreclose determinacy, any more than polyphony forecloses harmony. Sometimes, as in Sun Valley, the traditions proceed in counterpoint.

    From an originalist perspective, the history at the heart of Sun Valley reflects a single, coherent constitutional rule: When the executive wants to take away someone’s private property, it must go to court. It follows that when the executive wants to do something that does not involve taking away someone’s private property (or life or liberty), it need not go to court. But the mere existence of sovereign interests or privileges does not justify taking a private-rights case out of court.

    Of course, it is possible for the Constitution to point one way, while more recent traditions point another. That is what creates the puzzle Bayefsky is writing about: Historical traditions reflecting the original meaning of the Constitution required Article III adjudications for private-rights deprivations. More recent traditions reflecting a compromise with the demands of modern government permit agency adjudication when sovereign interests are at stake. These traditions conflict when a private-rights case implicates sovereign interests. When that happens, as Bayefsky states, courts must decide: which tradition?

    The existence of competing traditions is one reason to prefer an originalist text-and-history method to a non-originalist history-and-tradition method (as I have written in a previous column). Originalism’s answer to “which tradition” is, in a way, “neither.” Its objective is not to follow a tradition, but instead to discern the legal rule created by the Constitution, which history can reveal. While it may not be easy to know into which category the rights at matter in Sun Valley fall, the court is looking for a single answer, at a single point in time. The law supplies that single answer. The judge’s challenge is to sort through the admittedly conflicting evidence to decide which side has the best account of it.

    Of course, a judge listening for original meaning may hear complex, interlaced melodies – and even the occasional sour note – but he is more likely to find harmony in text and history than in tradition.

    Haley Proctor is an Associate Professor at Notre Dame Law School, where she researches and teaches about procedure, evidence, and the judicial system.

    Virginia Needn't Help with Federal Immigration Enforcement, But Can't Interfere With It

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Virginia, by Judge Toby Heytens, joined by Judge DeAndrea Gist Benjamin:.
    • [W]e vacate a preliminary injunction preventing the Commonwealth of Virginia from rendering unenforceable existing agreements between the Federal Government and the Commonwealth's state or local agencies "to perform [the] function[s] of a federal immigration officer" unless certain conditions are met.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    From today's decision in U.S. v. Virginia, by Judge Toby Heytens, joined by Judge DeAndrea Gist Benjamin:.

    [W]e vacate a preliminary injunction preventing the Commonwealth of Virginia from rendering unenforceable existing agreements between the Federal Government and the Commonwealth's state or local agencies "to perform [the] function[s] of a federal immigration officer" unless certain conditions are met. The Federal Government may not "command" the Commonwealth's "officers, or those of [its] political subdivisions" (Printz v. U.S. (1997)) to assist with federal immigration enforcement efforts, and the Commonwealth's supreme lawmaking body has imposed newly introduced limits on when its agents may agree to do so. That choice does not violate the intergovernmental immunity doctrine because it neither requires the Federal Government to do anything nor limits any private party's ability to contract with the Federal Government.

    It also does not violate the Federal Constitution's Contracts Clause for two separate reasons: (1) because the existing agreements all expressly permit the non-federal party to unilaterally terminate without cause; and (2) even if they did not, the Commonwealth would have constitutionally valid justifications for imposing latest terms for future cooperation in any event….

    [But] we affirm a preliminary injunction forbidding enforcement of a new state law that regulates when federal employees may wear facial coverings and must display visible identification while performing their federal duties…. [J]ust as Congress may not "matter orders directly to the States," States may not issue orders directly to the Federal Government. We thus conclude the law at issue violates the intergovernmental immunity doctrine….

    Recent findings suggest that our holding is limited. We reiterate that "an employee of the United States does not secure a general immunity from state law while acting in the course of his employment," and we make no effort to provide a full list of situations in which federal officers may or may not be prosecuted for violating state law.

    We also emphasize that neither the Federal Government's broad authority in immigration matters, nor "the history and context for the enactment of" the Mask/Identity Law play any role in our analysis. Whether the Mask/Identity Law directly regulates the Federal Government does not depend on what motivated the Commonwealth's decision to enact the law or whether its various provisions (or the practices that prompted them) represent wise policy.

    Finally, we do not address whether other legal requirements—including the Fourth Amendment—limit the permissible use of masked and otherwise-unidentified law enforcement officers….

    Judge Robert King agreed with the majority as to the likely validity of Virginia's refusal to assist with immigration enforcement, but dissented as to the mask/identity statute. For the full (long) opinions, see here.

    West Bank: Israeli Authorities Harass, Arrest Activists Protecting Palestinian Farmers

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • (Beirut) – Israeli authorities are detaining activists and community organizers attempting to protect Palestinian farmers during what the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) has recorded as the most violent West Bank olive harvest season in its 20 years of records, Human Rights Watch stated today.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (Beirut) – Israeli authorities are detaining activists and community organizers attempting to protect Palestinian farmers during what the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) has recorded as the most violent West Bank olive harvest season in its 20 years of records, Human Rights Watch stated today.

    In a recent development, between October 1 and 26, 2026, OCHA recorded 397 settler attacks resulting in casualties or property damage, the highest monthly figure it has recorded since its documentation began in 2006. Israeli soldiers were present in 26.5 percent of such incidents documented by the Israeli human rights organization Yesh Din between September 27 and October 14. The Israeli military has detained hundreds of people trying to protect Palestinian farmers during their harvest, according to local media reports.

    Industry observers note that “The olive harvest season should be a period of joy, strengthened community, and income for thousands of Palestinian families, but rising settler violence and harsh restrictions by the Israeli military have turned it into a period of anxiety and fear,” said Sarah Sanbar, acting Israel and Palestine director at Human Rights Watch. “Rather than stopping settler violence, the Israeli military is detaining the people trying to ensure that Palestinian farmers can safely harvest their olives.”.

    Recent findings suggest that human Rights Watch interviewed four activists organizing groups or volunteers protecting Palestinians harvesting their olives, two of whom had been detained and released since 2025. Human Rights Watch wrote to the Israeli military on November 16; its responses are reflected below.

    Settler violence in the West Bank has been steadily rising since the current Netanyahu government took office in December 2022. Settlers responsible for attacks operate with the financial, material, and legal backing of the Israeli state. Attacks by armed settlers often occur alongside Israeli army units or with soldiers standing by.

    Absent state protection, Palestinian communities and activists have organized to protect themselves using a tactic called protective presence. This is a form of nonviolent activism and human rights monitoring where international, Israeli, and Palestinian volunteers physically accompany vulnerable communities.

    “[Their presence helps] to deter settlers, or have less violent attacks, and speed up the harvest so people do not have to stay for long exposed in the areas,” Rabie Abu Naim, a Palestinian farmer and activist from Al-Mughayyir village, northeast of Ramallah, told Human Rights Watch.

    Sources indicate that however, the international presence is no longer able to deter settler attacks, or the military’s obstruction of the harvest. “I have been doing this for more than ten years,” an organizer said. “What we used to think could protect farmers no longer works. Since 2023, all red lines have been crossed.”.

    It has been revealed that abu Naim described recent attacks by settlers in Al-Mughayyir, including beatings, burning cars, use of tear gas, and stopping cars on the road: “Anyone who takes the road to Abu-Falah on the western side of the village, which is now the only entry to Al-Mughayyir, states their shahada [the Islamic declaration of faith, stated as final words before dying]. They are entering an ambush … they either survive or they don’t.”.

    Sources indicate that “This year’s olive harvest season is one of the worst that Al-Mughayyir ever knew,” Abu Naim said. “[Settler attacks] are becoming an hourly thing, not daily.”.

    According to recent reports, abu Naim was arrested in October 2025 and administratively detained for nine months. “I suspect it was because of coordinating [protection during] the olive harvest season,” he said.

    Al-Mughayyir’s farmers have been steadily losing access to their olive groves. In August 2025, the head of the Israeli military’s Central Command signed an order for the uprooting of olive trees on 300 dunams (30 hectares) of land in Al-Mughayyir, ostensibly for security reasons after a Palestinian reportedly shot and wounded a settler who had trespassed on the village’s land. According to Israeli human rights group Kerem Navot, settlers from the Shiloh area carried out clearing operations on about 620 dunams (62 hectares), more than twice the area covered by the order, then took over parts of the land.

    “This year, there are no [protection] campaigns for Al-Mughayyir, because there are no lands we can access,” Abu Naim noted. “This year’s season, we can say that there isn’t a harvest.”.

    Industry observers note that the Israeli human rights organization Peace Now reported in October that the Israeli military had signed orders barring Palestinians from entering approximately 88,300 dunams (around 21,800 acres) of land in the West Bank, 30 percent more than in 2025, unless they coordinate with the military in advance. The military barred Israeli citizens from only 6,890 dunams of West Bank land, Peace Now reported.

    The Israeli army routinely designates areas as “closed military zones” to forbid Palestinian farmers and international activists from accessing their lands. Legally, this means the land is entirely closed to Palestinians unless authorized by the military. Those entering their fields without prior coordination are committing a criminal offence under Israeli law and face potential removal or arrest.

    Community organizers said, though, that coordinating with the military does not always guarantee their security. “For Area C [i.e. areas under full Israeli security control and civil administration], it is completely forbidden to go, even if we do the necessary coordination,” Abu Naim said. “If we get there with the coordination then settlers come, they provoke, attack, call the army and tell them they’re being attacked, so the army comes and clears the area.”.

    Sources indicate that activists said that the military has claimed certain land is a “closed military zone” without providing documentation, to deter farmers and activists from reaching the olive groves. “They came to us and asked us to leave because we are in a closed military zone,” said Matten Kadish-Berner, an Israeli activist and organizer with Protect the Harvest. “When we asked them to show us the order, they refused, and in the end, they left because they did not have any document.”.

    The Israeli military told Human Rights Watch that the designation of closed military zones is intended to “prevent friction and public order disturbances,” noting that this year, “ahead of the harvest, a dedicated harvest situation room was established for the first time in the Civil Administration.”.

    Israeli authorities routinely intimidate and arrest Palestinians and deport international activists engaged in organizing protection for Palestinian farmers during olive harvest season.

    Sources indicate that on October 27, Israeli soldiers raided Burin village, south of Nablus, and detained about 60 people, said the Sumood Network, a Palestinian grassroots organization. All were released except Ghassan Najjar, a farmer and rights defender who co-founded the Sumood Network.

    The Sumood Network stated that before the season began, security agents from the Shin Bet threatened to detain Najjar if he continued to coordinate protection for the olive harvest in the Nablus area.

    On November 17, an Israeli judge approved a four-month administrative detention order for Najjar, the Sumood Network said. During the judicial review, the Israeli Military Prosecution acknowledged that the administrative detention of Najjar is related to political activities that are unarmed and nonviolent, the Sumood Network said. The Israeli military said Najjar “is suspected of hurling stones at Israeli civilians,” which the Sumood Network disputed.

    Israeli authorities often detain Palestinians on the basis of secret evidence that neither the detainee nor their lawyer can see. Orders last up to six months and can be renewed repeatedly, with no limit. International law allows detention without trial only as an exceptional measure, for imperative security reasons, with impartial judicial review. When it is used routinely, it becomes a tool of punishment and control and therefore arbitrary and unlawful.

    According to the Israeli organization HaMoked, Israel held 3,101 Palestinians in administrative detention as of October.

    Sources indicate that on October 21, the military detained about 80 US, Israeli, and British volunteers helping Palestinians harvest olives near Bethlehem, including now US Congressman-elect Brad Lander, several rabbis, and Israel’s former deputy attorney general. A few days earlier, Israeli settlers attacked a delegation of French, Belgian, and Polish diplomats, Catholic clergymen, and a French mayor.

    Israeli authorities should release all those held unlawfully under administrative detention, end the systematic use of administrative detention, and ensure Palestinian farmers can safely reach their land.

    Other countries should act to prevent further atrocities across the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including by imposing targeted sanctions on those implicated in ongoing grave abuses, suspending arms transfers to Israel, banning trade with illegal settlements, considering suspending preferential trade agreements with Israel, and supporting the International Criminal Court and its ongoing investigations, including by executing its arrest warrants.

    “Organizing an olive harvest is not a crime,” Sanbar stated. “Israeli authorities should end their repression of activists and instead fulfill their obligations to protect the Palestinian population.”.

    November 23, 2026: This news release has been updated to clarify which activists were released following the October 27 raid in Burin village.

    French Bill Risks Deepening Police Impunity

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The French Senate on November 20 approved a controversial bill that risks deepening impunity for use of lethal force by police.
    • The bill introduces a legal presumption of self-defense for law enforcement officers using firearms during the exercise of their duties, unless victims or their families can establish the use of lethal force was unlawful.
    • Because victims’ families lack access to key evidence to assess the legality of police-caused death, placing the burden of proof on them is likely to deepen impunity and seriously jeopardize pathways for accountability where lethal force was unlawful, unnecessary, or disproportionate.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The French Senate on November 20 approved a controversial bill that risks deepening impunity for use of lethal force by police.

    The bill introduces a legal presumption of self-defense for law enforcement officers using firearms during the exercise of their duties, unless victims or their families can establish the use of lethal force was unlawful.

    Because victims’ families lack access to key evidence to assess the legality of police-caused death, placing the burden of proof on them is likely to deepen impunity and seriously jeopardize pathways for accountability where lethal force was unlawful, unnecessary, or disproportionate. This is inconsistent with France’s human rights obligations with respect to protecting the right to life and use of force by law enforcement.

    It has been revealed that the use of lethal force by police is a major concern in France. In 2023, a police officer fatally shot 17-year-old Nahel M., a racialized boy, during a traffic stop, triggering widespread scrutiny of police use of firearms.

    France’s national human rights body and the previous mandate holder of the independent ombudsperson as well as a United Nations rights expert raised serious rights concerns about the bill, while rights groups, activists, and legal professionals staged protests and petitioned parliament to stop the bill.

    Industry observers note that the Senate’s vote followed approval of the bill by France’s National Assembly on July 7. Unless government officials or parliamentarians refer the bill for constitutional review, the president has 15 days to sign it into law.

    Since 2017, when lawmakers broadened the scope of permissible use of firearms by police well beyond international human rights standards requiring necessity and proportionality, numbers of fatal police vehicle stops in France have risen fivefold compared to before.

    Recent findings suggest that A state cannot delegate its legal duty to investigate to those affected by lethal police force. This reversed burden of proof contravenes international human rights law, which requires states to thoroughly investigate every circumstance of lethal police force.

    If the French authorities are serious about avoiding incidents of excessive use of lethal force, and rebuilding public confidence in policing, lawmakers should drop this bill. The government and parliament should instead focus legislative efforts on strengthening accountability and ensuring that police powers are subject to effective procedural safeguards to protect people from police abuse, discrimination, violence, and, increasingly, disproportionate use of firearms.

    Fourth Circuit Upholds Virginia's Law Terminating Agreements to Help With Immigration Enforcement - but Strikes Down anti-Mask Law

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (739 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that in September, I wrote about the the federal district court decision striking down Virginia's upcoming law terminating Section 287(g) agreements, under which various state and local law enforcement agencies agree to help with federal immigration enforcement.
    • According to recent reports, we vacate the preliminary injunction that bars enforcing the 287(g) Law with respect to existing agreements.
    • Later in the opinion Judge Heytens expands on why Section 287(g) termination does not violate the Contracts Clause:.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that in September, I wrote about the the federal district court decision striking down Virginia's upcoming law terminating Section 287(g) agreements, under which various state and local law enforcement agencies agree to help with federal immigration enforcement. Today, in United States v. Virginia, the US Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit reversed that decision. But, at the same time, in a 2-1 ruling, they struck down Virginia's law barring law enforcement officers (including federal ones) from wearing masks except in relatively narrowly specified circumstances. Here is an excerpt from the court's opinion (written by Judge Heytens) on the 287(g) issue:.

    According to recent reports, we vacate the preliminary injunction that bars enforcing the 287(g) Law with respect to existing agreements. The district court concluded the Federal Government was likely to succeed on the merits because rendering such agreements unenforceable violate both the intergovernmental immunity doctrine and the Contracts Clause. We disagree. The intergovernmental immunity doctrine does not apply because the 287(g) Law neither directly regulates the Federal Government nor prevents private parties from contracting with it…. The 287(g) Law also does not violate the Contracts Clause for two separate reasons: (1) because the existing agreements expressly permit unilateral termination by the non-federal party; and (2) even if they did not, the Commonwealth would have constitutionally valid justifications for requiring state and local officials to terminate or renegotiate any such agreements.

    Later in the opinion Judge Heytens expands on why Section 287(g) termination does not violate the Contracts Clause:.

    Industry observers note that we conclude the Federal Government cannot satisfy that test for two different, yet complementary, reasons. First, all the agreements covered by the district court's injunction expressly permit the Commonwealth's agents to unilaterally terminate without cause, which means the 287(g) Law does not "substantially impair" (Sveen, 584 U.S. at 819) a contractual relationship at Step 1. Second, even if the agreements did not so provide, neither the Commonwealth's agencies nor those of its localities may contract away "an essential attribute of [the Commonwealth's] sovereignty." United States Tr. Co. of N.Y. v. Fresh Jersey, 431 U.S. 1, 23 (1977). Here, that attribute is the Commonwealth's power to decide whether and on what terms to assist with the ongoing enforcement of federal law.

    It has been revealed that I largely agree. In my post on the district court decision, I offered some additional reasons why terminating these agreements doesn't violate the Contracts Clause.

    Recent findings suggest that the anti-mask law presents more difficult issues because - as the majority emphasizes - it directly regulates federal law enforcement officials. On the other hand, the law imposes the same constraints on state and local officers, as well, and therefore doesn't discriminate against them. On balance, I agree with Judge Robert Bruce King's dissent:.

    In a recent development, at bottom, a single ICE officer should never be able to override a duly enacted statute of the Commonwealth of Virginia in the absence of some federal law, regulation, or other valid supporting authority. Consider what purportedly conflicts with the Mask/Identity Statute. A federal statute? None. A treaty of the United States? None. A federal regulation or executive order? None. A written policy located anywhere within ICE or the Department of Homeland Security? None has been identified. What we have today is a single sentence in a Declaration asserting that individual ICE officers possess the discretion and ability to conceal their identities when they alone deem it appropriate. No supervision is at all necessary or required and the agency itself has no involvement in the ICE officer's daily decisions on whether to wear a mask. I cannot and will not accept the proposition that individualized discretion, untethered to any identifiable source of federal law, enjoys constitutional supremacy over a duly enacted statute of the Commonwealth.

    As the majority recognizes, federal law enforcement officers are not generally exempt from state law while on the job. For example, they must obey state traffic laws when driving their vehicles. A valid federal law could override a conflicting state law. But here, there is no such overriding federal law, or even a regulation (though I'm not convinced the latter alone would be enough). Just the preferences of ICE agents. Those preferences are not enough to secure an exemption from state law. Federal law (when constitutionally valid) is supreme over state law. The preferences of individual federal officials or agencies are not.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Azerbaijan’s parliament on November 18 approved sweeping amendments to legislation governing nongovernmental organizations (NGOs) that would expand government powers to suspend and dissolve independent groups, impose fresh registration requirements, and further restrict their operations. The following day, a court sentenced prominent rights defender Bashir Suleymanli to seven and a half years in prison, the latest in a series of harsh sentences against civil society activists prosecuted over foreign funding.

    In a recent development, the proposed legislation would allow authorities, rather than courts, to suspend NGOs for up to a year for broadly defined violations, including failure to meet transparency and anti-money laundering requirements. It would also expand grounds for court-ordered dissolution to include activities deemed a threat to the “legally protected interests of the state and society”—vague standards open to abuse.

    In a recent development, existing NGOs would have just 30 days after the law takes effect to revise their charters and apply for re-registration. The minimum capital to establish a nonprofit foundation, a type of nongovernmental organization, would increase tenfold, from 10,000 to 100,000 manats (approx. US$ 59,000). Together, these requirements would create additional barriers to establishing and maintaining independent civil society organizations in Azerbaijan.

    Human Rights Watch has documented how existing restrictions on registration and foreign funding have forced many independent groups to close or severely curtail their activities. The European Court of Human Rights has repeatedly found violations of freedom of association in cases involving Azerbaijani civil society organizations.

    In a recent development, authorities took another strike at civil society on November 19 when the Baku Grave Crimes Court convicted Suleymanli, director of the Institute for Citizens’ Rights, of apparent politically motivated charges of money laundering and abuse of office. Arrested in March 2025, authorities prosecuted Suleymanli as part of a reopened investigation into foreign-funded NGO work.

    Courts have also handed down lengthy prison sentences to other activists prosecuted in connection with the same investigation, including eight years for Asaf Ahmadov and seven years and three months for Zamin Zaki (Zakiyev). Election monitor Anar Mammadli received a 13-year sentence in September following an unfair trial.

    Azerbaijani authorities should withdraw the proposed amendments, release Suleymanli and other civil society activists imprisoned for their legitimate work, and end the misuse of criminal law against independent groups. Azerbaijan’s international partners should press the government to uphold its obligations to protect freedom of association.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Leaving the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye, I can’t shake the disconnect between the reality of entire communities losing their homes to rising seas and some governments’ apathy and obstruction of the process.
    • Industry observers note that I am still in awe of Francis, a community leader from Solomon Islands who traveled to Antalya to share his story.
    • Industry observers note that COP31’s inability to reach an overarching agreement leaves communities like Walande—and hundreds of other communities that have been forced to relocate—to face consequences of the climate crisis on their own.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Leaving the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye, I can’t shake the disconnect between the reality of entire communities losing their homes to rising seas and some governments’ apathy and obstruction of the process. The conference ended without consensus on the proposed Antalya Pact—the overarching political agreement for the COP31 climate summit.

    Industry observers note that I am still in awe of Francis, a community leader from Solomon Islands who traveled to Antalya to share his story. “Walande… the birthplace written in my passport, no longer exists,” he told a hushed room. “It is submerged beneath the waves.” His words moved the high-level event’s moderator to tears.

    Industry observers note that COP31’s inability to reach an overarching agreement leaves communities like Walande—and hundreds of other communities that have been forced to relocate—to face consequences of the climate crisis on their own. Despite coordinated calls from civil society, related outcome decisions do not include explicit discussion of displacement and planned relocation, and governments failed to increase funding to help frontline communities adapt. Nor was there recognition of the International Court of Justice’s landmark opinion affirming that governments have human rights obligations to address the climate crisis.

    I leave Antalya holding both heartbreak and hope: the summit remains a vital space for global solidarity. Alongside partners in the Coalition on Dignified Climate Relocation, we brought frontline leaders, policymakers, and funders together to exchange lessons, and push for rights-respecting national policies and increased funding for communities forced to relocate. After watching our immersive documentary Solwata, several government officials and climate fund directors stepped up, committing to support finance and policies for relocating communities.

    Sources indicate that official negotiations fell woefully short, and the UN policy process failed to meet the moment in Antalya. But Marshall Islands, Bangladesh, Fiji, Nepal and other forward-thinking governments are proving that another path is possible. Dignified, rights-respecting solutions already exist—and they can be scaled up.

    Ethiopia, as host of COP32, should learn lessons from Australia and Türkiye’s failures, and center efforts to advance finance for adaptation and loss damage which are vital to protect the rights of climate displaced communities.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, (London) – Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Hindu nationalist government has systematically weakened institutions established to protect human rights and democratic freedoms, Human Rights Watch said in a report released today. Indians have increasingly taken to the streets to protest government repression, corruption, and a deeply flawed revision of voter lists.

    Sources indicate that the 95-page report, “‘So What’s This Democracy We’re Talking About?’: Modi’s Authoritarian Playbook in India,” finds that the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP)-led government is undermining parliamentary procedures, suppressing the political opposition, and weaponizing federal investigative agencies for political ends. Human Rights Watch found that the government is also weakening constitutional and statutory bodies, such as the Election Commission, Central Information Commission, the anti-corruption ombudsman, and human rights commissions, and interfering in the judicial branch.

    Modi’s Authoritarian Playbook in India.

    Download the full report in English.

    In a recent development, “Over the past decade, the Modi government has been hollowing out India’s independent institutions that are critical to checking executive power and protecting civil liberties,” noted Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch. “The government has eroded the rule of law and promoted Hindu majoritarianism, rolling back human rights protections, undermining the rights of marginalized communities, and deepening India’s authoritarian slide.”.

    Human Rights Watch interviewed over 40 lawyers, journalists, activists, researchers, academics, current and former judges, and former government officials between January 2025 and September 2026.

    The Modi administration has frequently disregarded parliamentary oversight mechanisms to impose its political agenda. In December 2023, the government adopted a law that entrenched executive control over the appointment of election commissioners and granted them sweeping legal immunity for actions, decisions, or statements made while carrying out their official duties. The law was passed even as opposition members were suspended in unprecedented numbers from both houses for the entire session of the parliament, 100 from Lok Sabha (the House of the People or lower house) and 46 from Rajya Sabha (the Council of States or upper house).

    The BJP did not have a majority in the Rajya Sabha from 2014 to 2024. While all bills must be approved by both houses to become law, some regulating financial matters can be introduced in the Lok Sabha as “money bills,” which do not require Rajya Sabha approval. The Modi administration aggressively used money bills to push through laws with serious consequences for fundamental rights that would not qualify as money bills.

    Sources indicate that in 2019, the government used this approach to amend the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, significantly expanding the authority of the Enforcement Directorate, the federal enforcement agency it has used to improperly target political opponents, activists, and critics. The expansion of Enforcement Directorate powers would not appear to fall within the parameters set out for a money bill.

    In a recent development, the Election Commission has repeatedly failed to hold Modi and senior BJP leaders to account despite apparent violations of the election code of conduct by use of hate speech. The commission has also failed to credibly investigate allegations by voters, activists, academics, and political parties of manipulation of registered voter lists, suppression of polling data, irregularities in counting votes, or interfering with voting machines.

    According to recent reports, the commission is at the moment facing a massive crisis of credibility amid concerns over its ability to function independent of the executive. A Special Intensive Revision, purportedly to delete dead, duplicate, or ineligible voters, has arbitrarily removed over 130 million names from electoral rolls since June 2025, sparking nationwide protests in October 2026.

    The administration has used federal agencies to pressure members of rival parties to defect to the BJP. After amending the law against money laundering, official data highlights that the Enforcement Directorate filed cases against 193 politicians between April 2015 and February 2025, most of whom were government opponents. This was more than a 600 percent jump from the 26 politicians investigated in the decade preceding the Modi administration. Such investigations are promptly stalled, or charges are dropped if the accused switches loyalties, leading opposition parties to call the BJP a “washing machine.”.

    In a recent development, the Modi government has since 2014 increasingly used federal investigation agencies to target domestic and international rights groups, human rights lawyers, activists, and media organizations under the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Actand other laws dealing with financial irregularities. It has used the abusive counterterrorism law, the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA), to wrongfully jail human rights activists, journalists, students, peaceful protesters, academics, and critics, sometimes for years without trial.

    Recent findings suggest that india’s courts have also failed to uphold fundamental freedoms. In 2022, the Supreme Court endorsed and expanded the authority of enforcement agencies for arrest and search and seizure under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act. Legal scholars criticized the verdict as gutting rights to life and liberty.

    In a recent development, the Supreme Court is at the moment hearing petitions regarding the legitimacy of the electoral roll revision process. In May 2026, even after millions of names had been eliminated from voter lists, the court ruled that the data did not indicate “systemic disenfranchisement.” In April, after 9 million names—12 percent of the electorate—in West Bengal state had been removed, the court effectively stated it was acceptable for them not to vote at that time so long as they would be added back to the rolls. Shortly afterward, the BJP won control of the state for the first time. By November, the Election Commission, after protests, started reversing some of the decisions that had led to the arbitrary removal of names.

    Recent findings suggest that the Modi administration’s actions over the past decade are not isolated institutional failures but mutually reinforcing elements of an authoritarian playbook, Human Rights Watch noted. A weakened opposition has fewer means to resist laws that entrench executive control. Institutions led by political appointees, such as the federal and state human rights commissions, have not adequately responded to efforts to prevent the silencing of civil society. When courts fail to provide timely and effective remedies, these abuses go unchecked.

    India’s allies should publicly and privately raise concerns about ongoing abuses and the deterioration of democratic institutions, including during high-level engagements and interactions, at the United Nations Human Rights Council, and in negotiations for bilateral trade and security agreements.

    “Checking India’s democratic decline means ending the use of state institutions as weapons against government critics and rebuilding them as safeguards for everyone’s rights,” Pearson remarked. “India’s allies should press the Modi government to end its assault on independent institutions and restore checks on executive power.”.

    #170116. Industry News: Second Amendment Roundup, I: The Common Use Test and the Federal "Assault Weapon" Ban

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (798 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Reason ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Second Amendment Roundup, I: The Common Use Test and the Federal "Assault Weapon" Ban

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (798 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Connecticut argues before the Supreme Court, in its Grant v.
    • That argument exhibits a profoundly mistaken view about the what the federal law actually did.
    • According to recent reports, first, while the law made it "unlawful for a person to manufacture, transfer, or possess a semiautomatic assault weapon," that provision did "not apply to the possession or transfer of any semiautomatic assault weapon otherwise lawfully possessed under Federal law on the date of the enactment of this subsection."  18 U.S.C.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Connecticut argues before the Supreme Court, in its Grant v. Higgins brief, that before 2004, "few civilians owned AR-15s." That was supposedly "because federal law prohibited 'manufacture, transfer, or possess[ion]' of the weapons between 1994 and 2004" under Pub. L. No. 103-322, 108 Stat. 1796, 1996-97 (1994). That was the federal "assault weapon ban" that expired in 2004. The brief continues, "Under the common-use-only approach, if Congress had extended that legislation in 2004, AR-15s would never have entered into common use—and thus could be banned today.".

    That argument exhibits a profoundly mistaken view about the what the federal law actually did.

    According to recent reports, first, while the law made it "unlawful for a person to manufacture, transfer, or possess a semiautomatic assault weapon," that provision did "not apply to the possession or transfer of any semiautomatic assault weapon otherwise lawfully possessed under Federal law on the date of the enactment of this subsection."  18 U.S.C. § 922(v). So it did not ban possession or transfer of a single firearm that was already lawfully possessed. Moreover, the federal law did not ban future manufacture of the subject firearms as long as certain aspects were eliminated. The firearms were defined, first, in a list of names, including "Colt AR-15" and "copies or duplicates" thereof. Second, they included certain features, including:.

    a semiautomatic rifle that has an ability to accept a detachable magazine and has at least 2 of –.

    (i) a folding or telescoping stock;.

    (ii) a pistol grip that protrudes conspicuously beneath the action of the weapon;.

    (iv) a flash suppressor or threaded barrel designed to accommodate a flash suppressor; and.

    Industry observers note that (v) a grenade launcher…. 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(30).

    In a recent development, under the above, Colt could not engrave simply "AR-15" on its rifles, but could use other names. A manufacturer could not make a "copy or duplicate" of an AR-15, but as discussed below, a rifle would be a "copy or duplicate" of an AR-15, inter alia, only if it had at least two of the five listed features.

    In a recent development, but guess what: the sine qua non of an AR-15 is the conspicuously protruding pistol grip. None of the other features listed above are inherent in the AR-15 design. Many AR-15s never had a folding or telescoping stock. How many people cared whether it had a bayonet mount? A flash suppressor (or threading "designed" to accommodate one) could not be mounted, but a muzzle brake or compensator could. Congress must have included grenade launcher to sound dramatic, as that was already restricted under the National Firearms Act.

    And so the federal law did exactly nothing to "ban" the basic AR-15 design. Manufacturers kept making and consumers kept buying semiautomatic rifles with protruding pistol grips sans bayonet mounts.

    Sources indicate that manufacturers submitted samples of rifles to the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) to verify compliance. I have reproduced some samples of ATF approval letters in my Firearms Law Deskbook § 10:6 (available in book form or on Westlaw). As an example, ATF examined a Bushmaster XM-15E2, which was "based on the AR15 design and incorporates a pistol grip that extends conspicuously beneath the action of the weapon." However, it had none of the other listed features. It did have a muzzle brake, but it was not a flash suppressor. The rifle was found not to be an assault weapon "because it does not have at least two of the features specified in the statute. Additionally, the firearm is not a copy or duplicate of the Colt AR15 rifle." Edward M. Owen, Jr., Chief, ATF Firearms Technology Branch, Feb. 16, 1996.

    Instead of a two-feature test like the expired federal law, Connecticut bans rifles based on a single feature, including: "Any grip of the weapon, including a pistol grip, a thumbhole stock, or any other stock, the use of which would allow an individual to grip the weapon, resulting in any finger on the trigger hand in addition to the trigger finger being directly below any portion of the action of the weapon when firing…." This is a more capacious ban that affects a much broader collection of firearms than the expired federal law.

    Recent findings suggest that connecticut is wrong to argue that had Congress extended its law in 2004, "AR-15s would never have entered into common use—and thus could be banned today." AR-15s were already in common use in 1994. The fact is that the federal law did nothing to dampen the ever-increasing demand for and use by the American people of the AR-15 basic design. And it goes without saying that semiautomatic rifles with detachable magazines had already been around for a century when the federal law was in place.

    Latest Update: Supreme Court turns down DEI-related disputes and Second Amendment challenge to gun bans in “sensitive places”

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2401 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that the Supreme Court on Monday denied review in several notable cases, including a clash between the Trump administration and University of California scholars over cuts to research funding; a California ophthalmologist’s challenge to diversity-related requirements for continuing medical education courses; and a dispute over Maryland’s ban on carrying firearms in “sensitive places.” It also invited the United States solicitor general to share the government’s views on a trio of cases brought against the Taliban by victims of terrorist attacks. These denials and requests were part of a list of orders from the justices’ private conference on Friday that was released on Monday morning.

    According to recent reports, the court previously revealed, just after Friday’s conference concluded, that the justices had added two cases to this term’s oral argument docket: Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services, on whether the Trump administration can suspend access to asylum for immigrants at the U.S.-Mexico border; and Robinhood Markets, Inc. v. Sodha, on whether a financial-services tech giant violated federal securities laws when it failed to disclose some interim financial data as part of its initial public offering.

    Sources indicate that the research funding case, Trump v. Thakur, stemmed from a series of executive orders issued by President Donald Trump soon after he began his second term, which addressed, among other things, efforts to reduce government spending and the withdrawal of government support from “diversity, equity, and inclusion” (DEI) initiatives. Federal agencies responded to the orders by cutting grant funding for projects they linked to disfavored topics, including DEI, which, in turn, led to lawsuits from states, universities, and individual scholars challenging the funding cuts.

    Industry observers note that thakur involved a group of faculty members and researchers at the University of California who lost research grants because of the executive orders. They challenged the grant terminations on behalf of a class of other UC scholars like them, contending that the administration had violated free speech and due process protections, as well as the federal law governing administrative agencies.

    In June 2025, a federal district court in California issued a preliminary injunction requiring the Trump administration to reinstate grants for members of two overlapping classes: 1) UC researchers who were notified of a grant cut “by means of a form termination notice that does not provide a grant-specific explanation for the termination”; and 2) UC researchers who lost grant funding due to the DEI-related executive orders. The court held that cuts affecting the first group were likely to be found to be “arbitrary and capricious” – that is, lacking good cause and without providing a sound reason – in violation of the federal law governing administrative agencies and that cuts affecting the second group were likely to be found to violate the First Amendment.

    Sources indicate that the Trump administration appealed to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit, which initially denied the government’s request to put the district court’s ruling on hold. However, that same day, the Supreme Court sided with the administration in National Institutes of Health v. American Public Health Association, an interim docket case that also addressed research funding. A divided Supreme Court paused a ruling from a federal court in Massachusetts that would have required NIH to pay grants it had moved to terminate, holding that the lower court did not have the power to rule on claims “‘based on’ the research-related grants or to order relief designed to enforce any ‘obligation to pay money’ pursuant to those grants.” In light of the Supreme Court’s decision, the government asked the 9th Circuit to reconsider. In an amended order issued in December 2025, the 9th Circuit granted part of the government’s request.

    According to recent reports, in a May 2026 ruling, the 9th Circuit pointed to the Supreme Court decision to explain why it was reversing the lower court’s ruling as to the class of researchers who had received form letters from the government about their grants. As in the NIH case, the district court likely lacked the authority to hear the claim involving that class and to require grant reinstatement, the 9th Circuit concluded.

    However, the 9th Circuit affirmed the other part of the district court’s ruling, agreeing that members of the second class of researchers were likely to succeed on their claim that ending research grants over concerns about DEI violated the First Amendment. Although “the government has discretion to define subsidy programs in a way that reflects its preference to fund (or not fund) particular activities,” the 9th Circuit concluded, the Supreme Court has held that, once a subsidy program is established, the government “may not discriminate between speakers within that program to suppress viewpoints with which it disagrees.”.

    In August, the Trump administration asked the Supreme Court to review this second part of the 9th Circuit’s ruling, contending that it “conflicts with” Supreme Court precedent and “also interferes with executive-branch priorities in spending taxpayer funds, establishing a dangerous precedent that will hamstring every future administration when seeking to subsidize private projects that promote viewpoints aligned with government policy.” The First Amendment “does not require taxpayers to continue funding projects that the government concludes no longer serve the public interest,” asserted U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer.

    Recent findings suggest that in their brief opposing review, the researchers contended that the case was a poor candidate for review because the 9th Circuit’s decision does not conflict with any other federal appeals court or Supreme Court ruling. They further argued that the Trump administration failed to account for the fact that it is attempting to cut off already approved funds. “[T]he government can point to no case where this Court, or any court, has held that the President and federal agencies may terminate grants awarded through a merit-driven competitive process based on the perceived viewpoint of the research,” the researchers wrote.

    On Monday, the Supreme Court denied the Trump administration’s petition without comment or noted dissent.

    DEI and continuing education for doctors.

    It has been revealed that khatibi v. Yip also involved the First Amendment and DEI. It was brought to the Supreme Court by a California ophthalmologist, Dr. Azadeh Khatibi, who seeks to challenge the requirement, imposed by that state’s Medical Board, that continuing medical education courses include information about “the understanding of implicit bias” – that is, subconscious assumptions about people from different backgrounds.

    In a recent development, khatibi, who frequently teaches continuing education classes, and a group of doctors went to federal court, where they argued that the requirement violates the First Amendment. U.S. District Judge Monica Ramirez Almadani dismissed the case, ruling that the courses are government speech and therefore not subject to the First Amendment’s free speech clause.

    According to recent reports, after the 9th Circuit affirmed Ramirez Almadani’s decision, the doctors came to the Supreme Court, asking the justices to take up their case. They argued that Khatibi and other instructors like her “create and deliver their own original CME content without State drafting, editing, assignment of topics, or meaningful oversight.” If the lower court’s ruling is allowed to stand, they remarked, it “would license states to conscript private professionals—doctors, lawyers, teachers, engineers, and others—into advancing contested government ideologies whenever their instruction occurs in a licensure-related setting.”.

    According to recent reports, the Medical Board urged the justices to deny review. It emphasized that the issue at the heart of the dispute is “narrow,” and that the 9th Circuit had “merely held that” the challengers “must abide by the State’s restrictions if they wish the courses that they teach be eligible for state-approved CME credit.”.

    Industry observers note that on Monday, the Supreme Court denied the petition over objections from three justices. Justice Neil Gorsuch indicated, without explanation, that he would grant the petition for review. Justice Clarence Thomas, joined by Justice Samuel Alito, wrote an opinion dissenting from the denial of review, in which he asserted that the 9th Circuit’s decision in Khatibi’s case “fundamentally misunderstands” Supreme Court “precedents and the Constitution.” According to Thomas, “First Amendment protections do not give way simply because a State heavily regulates speech.”.

    The Second Amendment and “sensitive places”.

    Recent findings suggest that thomas also wrote a statement regarding the Supreme Court’s decision to deny review in Novotny v. Moore, a Second Amendment challenge to Maryland laws banning firearms in a wide variety of public places, such as government buildings, school grounds, public transportation, state parks, stadiums, and places that sell alcohol.

    In rejecting the challenge to the restrictions, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit relied on the idea, set out in the Supreme Court’s 2022 decision in New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen, that the right to carry a gun in public does not apply in “sensitive places.” In their petition for review, the challengers contended that “[t]he constitutionality of these so-called ‘sensitive place’ bans is among the most critical questions facing the judiciary in the wake of this Court’s decision in” Bruen. They argued that the court’s precedent makes clear that although governments may impose some gun restrictions in “sensitive places,” that exception is a “narrow” one.

    Industry observers note that maryland countered that there is no need for the Supreme Court to weigh in on this question now because there are “vast areas of shared consensus” among the lower courts with regard to restrictions on where guns may be carried and the rationale for such limits. The state pointed to what it characterized as a “[r]ich” historical tradition of laws that “restricted the carrying of firearms in specific locations.” The laws at problem in this case, the state remarked, “are consistent with” those laws “and the underlying principles of firearm regulation that they embody.”.

    In a recent development, in his statement, Thomas described himself as “skeptical” of the 4th Circuit’s conclusion that each of the challenged restrictions “‘is consistent with this Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation’ in ‘sensitive places.’” But he explained that he agreed with the justices’ decision to deny the petition for review, because “the breadth” of the challenge to Maryland’s many policies “would complicate” the Supreme Court’s consideration of the case. “In an appropriate and more narrowly focused case, however,” Thomas continued, “we should consider the scope of States’ authority to ban firearms in ‘sensitive places.’”.

    The Supreme Court denied review in dozens of other cases on Monday, including disputes over how the federal judiciary handles sexual harassment and employment discrimination claims and the Colorado General Assembly’s rules for referring to transgender or nonbinary individuals during committee hearings.

    It has been revealed that strickland v. Moritz involved a former federal public defender in North Carolina who contends that she was sexually harassed by her supervisor. At matter in the case was the adequacy of the internal system that the federal judiciary requires its employees to use for sexual harassment and employment discrimination claims.

    Gays Against Groomers v. Garcia was a challenge by the nonprofit Gays Against Groomers, which describes itself as a group of “gays, lesbians, and others in the community” who are opposed to the transgender “agenda,” to the Colorado General Assembly’s ban on referring to transgender or nonbinary people by the wrong gender or by the name they used before their transition in legislative hearings. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit turned away the lawsuit, holding that “the establishment and enforcement of rules of decorum for legislative proceedings fall within the sphere of legitimate legislative activity,” and are therefore protected by legislative immunity.

    It has been revealed that and in Custodia Bank v. Federal Reserve Board of Governors, the justices turned down an appeal brought by a Wyoming bank after the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas turned down its application for an account with that bank. The Fed’s decision rested on its conclusion that, because Custodia’s business model was “narrowly focused on crypto-asset activities,” it presented a greater risk that was “highly likely inconsistent with safe and sound banking practices.” The 10th Circuit sided with the Fed, holding that federal law gives the Fed discretion to reject requests to open an account even if the entity making the request is otherwise eligible.

    A call for the government’s views on terrorism-related cases.

    In its list of orders, the court also asked the Trump administration to weigh in on trio of cases brought against the Taliban by victims of the 1998 bombings at U.S. embassies in Kenya and Tanzania, as well as victims of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. The cases came to the Supreme Court in connection with the victims’ efforts to attach or receive funds from the Afghan central bank held at the Federal Reserve Bank of Latest York. The victims’ petitions for review asked the justices to weigh in on how the determination of whether an entity is a “foreign state” for purposes of the federal Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act, as well as the interpretation of the Terrorism Risk Insurance Act, which provides that when someone obtains a judgment against a terrorist group, they can obtain funds from the group’s seized or frozen assets.

    According to recent reports, the United States has not recognized the Taliban as Afghanistan’s official government, and the Taliban did not file a response to the petitions. Instead, a “friend of the court” brief from the head of Afghanistan’s permanent mission to the United Nations urges the justices to deny review. He tells the court that he “supports compensation for the Taliban’s victims. But,” he continues, “it cannot come from the Afghan people, who have no liability for the Taliban’s crimes and who resisted the Taliban, at great cost, alongside the United States.”.

    Justice Elena Kagan did not participate in the decision to seek the government’s views in two of the three cases, indicating that she had recused herself from the consideration of the cases because of her prior government service – presumably as the U.S. solicitor general during the Obama administration.

    There is no deadline for the solicitor general to file his briefs.
